authors.name: Parimelazhagar
authors.work: Paraphrased in English by an AI

summary.en: A poet praises his own god or the god suited to his subject. He says this is the second: the book treats three goals, each tied to one of the three first gods, so the praise is addressed to all three in common.
This chapter tells the greatness of rain, which by god’s command keeps the world going, and with it righteousness, wealth and pleasure. That explains why it follows the praise of god.

chapters.name: நீத்தார் பெருமை
chapters.title: The Greatness of Those Who Renounce

summary.en: This chapter tells the greatness of sages who have renounced completely. They are the ones who show the world righteousness and the rest as they truly are, so it follows the greatness of rain.

Of the three those sages teach, righteousness alone, unlike wealth and pleasure, yields this life, the next and release. So this chapter says it is stronger than they are, and that also explains its place.
This is the excellence of living with a wife. It follows the chapter on righteousness because it is the first of the two states in which righteousness is done.
This is the goodness of the wife, the companion of home life. That is why it follows the chapter on home life.
The twice-born owe three debts: to the sages, paid by study, to the gods, paid by sacrifice, and to the ancestors, paid only by begetting sons. This chapter is about having children to pay that debt.
He defines அன்பு as fondness for your wife, children and others connected to you, and says compassion for all beings grows from it.
This is caring for guests, expected and unexpected. He ranks it first among household duties, and places it after loving-kindness because only two people joined by loving-kindness can do it.
This means saying sweet words that show the gladness in your mind. Those who care for guests can’t do without it, so it follows that chapter.

chapters.name: செய்ந்நன்றியறிதல்
chapters.title: Remembering the Good Done to You

summary.en: This is not forgetting the good others have done you. It follows sweet speech because, for those who keep household righteousness, the one fault with no escape is destroying a kindness, and this guards against it.

This is standing even towards enemies, strangers and friends without slipping from righteousness. It follows the last chapter because remembering a kindness can tempt you to lean towards the one who did it.
This is holding body, speech and mind back from evil paths. It follows impartiality because it belongs to someone who sees their own faults as they see a stranger’s.
This is keeping the conduct laid down for your varna and stage of life. It follows restraint because only those who have restrained body, speech and mind can do it.
This is not wanting another man’s wife through the delusion of desire. It follows good conduct because it is found only in those who have good conduct.

He defines this as bearing it, and not doing the same back, when someone wrongs you for some cause or out of ignorance. It follows the chapter on another’s wife, to say you must bear even with those who leave the path.
He has already explained envy, at couplet 35. It is the opposite of bearing wrongs, so this chapter, which forbids it, follows that one.
He defines this as not thinking of seizing what belongs to others. It follows the chapter on envy, to say that beyond resenting what others have, even the thought of taking it is a fault.
He defines this as not running people down when they aren’t there. Faults of speech grow from faults of the mind, so it follows the chapters on envy and coveting.

He defines this as not saying words that bring no righteousness, wealth or pleasure to you or anyone. Householders can’t wholly avoid lies, and harsh words and backbiting are already dealt with, so useless words come next.
He defines this as being afraid to do what is sin. The chapter gathers up and forbids all the sins of the body, so it follows the chapter on useless words.

chapters.name: ஒப்புரவறிதல்
chapters.title: Knowing Your Duty to the World

summary.en: He defines this as knowing the way of the world and acting on it. The books don’t set it out as they do scriptural conduct: you must know it for yourself. After what to avoid in thought, word and deed, this turns to what remains to be done.
This means giving, without refusing, to the poor who ask. It looks to the next life, so it follows the duty to the world, which looks to this one.

This is the renown that arises in this world and doesn’t die, this life’s reward for those who don’t stray from the household righteousness told so far. It comes mostly from giving, so it follows that chapter.
He defines compassion as mercy that goes out naturally to all living beings, with no tie behind it. It matters to renunciation as loving-kindness does to household life, so it comes first.

He defines this as giving up eating flesh. Eating flesh keeps killing going and also comes from it, so it is both cause and result of that sin. It can’t go with compassion, so this chapter follows that one.

He defines austerity as bearing the pain of vows, such as cutting food and standing in sun, rain and cold so the mind won’t follow the senses, while tending other beings. It comes once refusing meat has ripened compassion.

He defines this as evil conduct that doesn’t fit austerity: lacking strength, someone wants again the pleasures of desire they gave up, yet keeps the garb. It follows austerity in order to forbid this.

He defines this as not thinking of taking by deceit anything that belongs to others. For a renouncer the thought is as bad as the act. It deals with faults over wealth, so it follows the chapter on faults of desire.
வாய்மை is the nature of truth. It forbids lying, which mostly springs from desire and wealth, so it follows the chapters on false conduct and on not stealing.
This means not getting angry even when you have cause. It forbids the anger that arises from lying, so it follows the chapter on truthfulness.
This means not harming any being, whether for gain, out of hatred or through carelessness. Harm happens without anger too, so it follows the chapter on anger.

This means not killing any living thing, from those with five senses to those with one, even by carelessness. It surpasses all the righteousness above and takes in what hasn’t been named, so it comes last.

Impermanence is the way that nothing that comes to be can last. Those who say what things are differ in many ways, but all accept this. Attachment doesn’t end until it is understood, so it comes first.
This means letting go of attachment to outer wealth and to the inner body, on seeing that neither lasts. That is also why it follows impermanence.
This means knowing birth, release and their causes as they are, without error or doubt. It too comes from holding to the one who has no attachment, so it follows renunciation.

Those who have cut off deeds past and future still have this body and its fruit, and old habit can draw the mind back to the senses. That thought is a seed of birth, to be cut off by constant knowledge of the truth.
He treats ஊழ் as the rule that the fruit of your deeds comes back to you, and says wealth and joy both turn on it.
This means the ruler’s good qualities and good deeds. The word இறை is used because he protects the world in the form of the gods who guard it.

This is the ruler learning the right books: on righteousness and statecraft, on elephants, horses, chariots and weapons. It sits among the chapters on rule, but it is spoken generally, because it benefits everyone.
This means the lowness that comes of not learning. Praising learning wasn’t enough on its own, so it is shown from the other side as well, after the chapter on learning.

This means hearing the learned explain the meaning of the books. It strengthens the knowledge of those who have learned and gives knowledge to those who haven’t, so it follows the chapters on learning and not learning.
This means having your own true understanding, alongside what comes from learning and listening.

This means a ruler keeping six faults out of himself: desire, anger, miserliness, false honour, excess joy and arrogance. Only those with understanding can see and remove them, so it follows that chapter.

A ruler fit to drive the cart of protection takes as helpers men of great wisdom, the ministers and priests who turn him from the bad path to the good and guard him from troubles sent by people or gods.
The petty are those who say good has no good in it and evil no evil, with rakes, libertines and actors. Such a group twists the mind and ruins both worlds, so joining it undoes the help of the great.
How a ruler examines each task before he does it. Once the great have become useful helpers he does this with them, so it follows the chapter on petty company.
A ruler who has settled on punishment among the means measures the four kinds of strength.
A ruler with the greater strength, setting out against his enemy, learns the time that suits the march.
A ruler who knows his strength and the time, setting out against his enemy, learns the ground on which he can win.
Testing ministers and others by their birth, character, understanding and deeds, then trusting them. A ruler marching on his enemy needs this so that work gets done and no one betrays him.
How a ruler learns which tasks the people he has come to trust can do, and employs them in those tasks.
A ruler holds his relatives close so that they don’t leave him. Having spoken of those who do his work, he turns here to the rest of his circle.
Not growing careless about guarding yourself or destroying your enemies, through delight in your looks, fortune or power. Kin are of use only where there is no such lapse.
The justice a ruler gives. It leans to neither side, like a straight rod, so it is called the sceptre. Only a ruler free of lapses can give it.
The leaning of a ruler’s justice, named again from the rod. It is the opposite of the straight sceptre, so it follows that chapter.
Not doing what frightens the people, what frightens his officers, or what leaves the ruler himself afraid. Such acts belong with the crooked sceptre, so this chapter follows it.

This is being unable to refuse what people familiar to you say, once you see them. It happens when your eye goes out to them, hence its name. It expands on what the chapter on not ruling by fear said, so it follows that chapter.
He says this means employing spies to learn what happens among enemies, neutrals and friends. A ruler needs it both to run his own land and to take others’, so it comes first.
He defines ஊக்கம் as being roused to act without the mind weakening. Whoever learns through spies what has happened must act on it and needs drive to do so, so this follows the chapter on spies.
He defines this as not slacking when you do what you have planned. Even those with drive can at times grow lazy through the pull of their nature, so this follows the chapter on drive.
He defines ஆள்வினை as unbroken, real effort. Getting rid of laziness is not enough, because work is only carried out by effort, so this follows the chapter on laziness.
He defines this as keeping the mind steady when trouble comes to someone striving at a task, whether it comes from god, from lack of wealth or from the strain on the body.
He defines this as the nature of a minister, meaning his qualities and his actions.
He defines this as being able to say the words that carry a minister’s work to the end he intends. It expands “speak with certainty” from K634, so it follows the chapter on the minister.
He defines this as work that yields not only wealth but righteousness and fame. Action must be good as well as speech, so this follows the chapter on speech.
He defines this as the firmness of mind needed by someone who is to carry clean work through to its end.
He defines this as the way a minister with such firmness carries out the work.

He defines this as the nature of those sent to other rulers to make peace or war. One kind frames his own words and equals a minister. The other repeats what he was told and has a quarter less of a minister’s qualities.
He defines this as how ministers should conduct themselves with rulers. “The qualities rulers desire” were asked of the envoy, so this follows that chapter.
He defines this as knowing what a ruler has in mind without being told. It comes here because no one who serves rulers can do without it.
He defines this as knowing the nature of the assembly around the ruler. When you speak on business you need this as well as reading his mind.
He defines this as having no fear when you speak before an assembly you have judged fit to hear you.
This chapter tells of the country, which the ruler and minister carry forward, and which the other parts of the state, such as the fortress, can’t do without.
The fortress belongs to the country, yet it is named as a part of the state on its own, because when enemies threaten ruin it protects both the country and the ruler.
This chapter tells how to make wealth, which is mostly gained through the country and guarded by the fortress.
The army, which wealth provides and which wins victories, takes two chapters. This first one is on what makes an army good.

chapters.name: படைச் செருக்கு
chapters.title: The Fierce Pride of an Army

summary.en: He defines this as an army’s surplus of valour.
Friendship helps a ruler in his work, as an army does. He gives it five chapters on what to do and twelve on what to avoid, and this is the first of the five.
You should befriend only those you have examined and found to have the marks given above. This chapter is on how to examine them.
He defines this as bearing the faults of friends because they are old friends. It follows the testing of friends because even tested friends have faults, and fate too makes them err.
Friendship that must be dropped, because its faults can’t be borne, takes two chapters. This first one is on friendship with people of bad character.
He defines this as the friendship of enemies who never join you at heart, but stay close outwardly until they get their chance.
He turns from friendship to enmity, which springs from anger and desire. Their root is delusion, treated in two chapters, and the first is folly: knowing nothing at all.
He turns to the other delusion: to have a small understanding, rate it as great, and refuse the sound words of those above you.
Of anger and desire, anger is the greater danger for rulers, so he begins with what anger brings. First comes strife: the discord that makes two sides fight and wear out their strength.
A ruler can’t be wholly without enemies, so the strife forbidden in general is prescribed here in one special case: enmity made worthwhile because the enemy has faults such as lack of understanding.
He weighs the fault of making unworthy enmity, which enemies to turn into friends or neutrals, what to do with each, how and when to remove the rest, and the harm of failing to.
This is the enmity that opens the way for the outer enemy and stays hidden inside until that enemy wins. It too must be removed.
This is not living in contempt of the great, meaning both rulers, great in power, and sages, great in penance. It closes the chapters on what anger brings.
What desire brings isn’t enmity outright, but it wrecks gain and brings ruin, so it is counted with enmity. First comes a man following the way of his wife, who should be following his.
This is the nature of women who sell their charms to anyone who pays, drawing no line between the fit and the unfit. It follows the faults that come from a man’s own wife.
In ruining conduct and understanding, liquor is like the women of the last chapter. This chapter tells the worth of not drinking it, by speaking of what it does.
Like drinking, gambling and illness come between a person and righteousness, wealth and pleasure. This chapter starts on those two with the nature of gambling.

Diseases come from past deeds and from causes such as unsuitable food and actions. Those from past deeds end only when the deeds are spent, so this chapter sets them aside and tells the medicine for the rest.
This is the character of those born in a high family. All four varnas can’t do without high birth, so this chapter comes first in its part.
He begins the qualities of the well-born with honour: never falling below your standing, and not staying alive when god brings you down. It comes first because it keeps their birth upright.

Greatness is the nature of the great, shown in doing what is hard, lacking arrogance and not speaking of others’ faults. These arise only where you don’t fall from your standing, so it follows honour.
This is being full of many good qualities and ruling them. It gathers the many qualities that don’t fall under greatness, so it follows that chapter.
This is knowing the nature of everyone and getting along with them, without slipping yourself from greatness and worth. That is why it comes after those chapters.
This is the nature of wealth that is no use to the one who earned it or to anyone else. The owner’s fault is laid on the wealth. The last couplet of the previous chapter pointed here.
This is the quality by which those raised high by worth, courtesy and the like feel shame at acts unworthy of them. That is why it follows those chapters.
This is the art of raising the family you were born into. It belongs to those who feel shame at falling low, so it follows the chapter on shame.
Ploughing belongs mostly to the cultivators’ varna and a little to merchants, and others may have it done for them. It is the effort that raises a family, so it follows that chapter.
Poverty is having none of the things that can be enjoyed.

Begging that leaves your honour whole is as good as not begging, and the books of righteousness say the body, which can reach release, is to be kept even this way. So this chapter forbids the utter renunciation that poverty ended on.
This is fear of the begging that costs you your honour.
This is the nature of the low, who have none of the qualities the earlier chapters stated or implied. So it comes after all of them.
She has left her companions to play in a grove, and he has left his young men to hunt. He comes on her alone, and tells how her beauty torments him. This happens at first sight, so it comes first.
He says this is the man reading the woman’s signs and her friend’s, and the friend reading both of theirs. The man struck by her beauty needs it if he is to reach her.
Having read her signs and come together with her, the man speaks of his delight in that union.
The man dresses her beauty in words of praise. It follows the delight in union, because that is when such praise arises.
The man and then the woman each say how great their love is. It follows the chapters on union and on her beauty, because such love arises from those.
Turned away and unable to bear it, the man tells her friend he has given up shame. The woman, wanting her love made known, tells her friend the same. This comes when love is at its height.
One who wants the secret love to go on tells her friend how the gossip helps. She and her friend, wanting marriage or elopement, tell him of it. It comes once shame has been given up.
After marriage he leaves her, for near or far, for righteousness, wealth or joy. This is her inability to bear it, spoken by her friend to him and by her to her friend.
She can’t bear the parting. Thinking always of the pain she suffers, she wastes away and grieves.
Her eyes suffer in their haste to see him. This comes after she has wasted away in grief.
பசப்பு is the change of colour that comes from being unable to bear parting, and this is the pain of it. It comes when she can’t see him.
She says the overflowing grief is hers alone and not his, because he left for righteousness and wealth. It belongs to the woman who has suffered pallor.
Remembering the joy of their past union, she feels alone, and so does he in his war camp.
She tells her friend about the dream she saw. She dreamed it because she thought of him so much while awake, so this chapter follows the one on lamenting in memory.
When evening comes, she sees it and grieves. She has got through the day on the strength of her dream, so this chapter follows the one on the dream.
Her eyes, arms, forehead and other features lose their beauty. This happens when grief is at its height, so the chapter follows the one on grieving at evening.
Overwhelmed and with nothing to hold on to, she speaks to her heart, not knowing what to do. This comes once her features have lost their beauty, so it follows that chapter.

Overwhelmed by longing, she can’t hold back what she should keep to herself, and lets it out. Reserve means others don’t learn your secrets. It fails because she spoke to her heart, so this chapter follows that one.

In a long separation, he and she each hurry with longing to see the other. He rejects the view that this is only her longing for him. Her words here come from lost reserve, so the chapter follows that one.
He, she and her friend each make their hidden intent known to one another. This happens once he has come back and they are together, so the chapter follows the one on longing to meet.
He and she both hurry towards union. She has made his intent to leave known, yet the eagerness rises in her from her own great longing, so this chapter follows the one on making signs known.
She sulks with her heart, which longs for union and won’t think of sulking even when there is cause, and he does the same with his. That also explains the chapter’s place here.
With neither heart hurrying to union and both meaning to sulk, the two sulk with each other. That also explains the chapter’s place here.
When he and she are together in bed she has no cause to sulk, but her love runs so high that she imagines a fine cause, lays it on him and sulks. That also explains the chapter’s place here.
When sulking has made union sweeter, she and he each delight in the sulking.

padaccheda.m: எழுத்துக்கள் எல்லாம் அகரமாகிய முதலை உடையன
அதுபோல உலகம் ஆதிபகவனாகிய 1 முதலை உடைத்து

en.1: As all letters begin with A, the world begins with the First Lord.
en.2: All letters have A as their first, and the world likewise has the First Lord. A leads because it arises by nature as bare sound, not by change. The Lord leads because he knows everything by nature, not by learning. “All letters” includes Sanskrit, and “world” means living beings. The seen world is named to show that the unseen god exists.

padaccheda.m: (எல்லா நூல்களையும் கற்றவர்க்கு) அக்கல்வி அறிவினாலாய பயன் யாது? வால் அறிவன் நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின் = மெய்யுணர்வினை உடையானது நல்ல தாள்களைத் தொழாராயின்

en.1: What use is learning to those who won’t worship the good feet of the one whose knowledge is pure?
en.2: What use is the learning of someone who has read every book, if they don’t worship the good feet of the one with true knowledge? None. The feet are good because they cure the disease of birth. The use of scriptural knowledge is to worship his feet and so end birth.

padaccheda.w: மலர் மிசை ஏகினான் மாண் அடி சேர்ந்தார்
padaccheda.m: மலரின்கண்ணே சென்றவனது மாட்சிமைப்பட்ட அடிகளைச் சேர்ந்தார்
(எல்லா உலகிற்கும்) மேலாய வீட்டுலகின்கண் அழிவின்றி வாழ்வார்

en.1: Those who reach the noble feet of the one who walked on the flower will live long on the earth.
en.2: Those who reach the glorious feet of the one who goes upon the flower live forever in the world of release, above all worlds. The flower is the heart’s lotus: he hurries there, in the form they imagine, for those who think of him with love. To reach his feet is to think of him without a break. Some give this to another god because of the title “walker on flowers”.

reading.note: The words say long life “on the earth”. He takes நிலமிசை as above all worlds, the world of release, and the flower as the heart.

padaccheda.m: (ஒரு பொருளையும்) விழைதலும் வெறுத்தலும் இல்லாதவன் அடியைச் சேர்ந்தார்க்கு
எக்காலத்தும் (பிறவித்) துன்பங்கள் உளவாகா

en.1: Those who reach the feet of the one who wants nothing and rejects nothing will have no suffering, ever.
en.2: Those who reach the feet of the one who neither longs for nor hates anything have no suffering of birth at any time. That suffering is of three kinds: from yourself, from other beings and from the gods. Those who reach his feet are also free of longing and hatred, so the three sufferings, which come from those two, don’t arise.

padaccheda.m: மயக்கத்தைப் பற்றிவரும் (நல்வினை தீவினை என்னும்) இரண்டுவினையும் உளவாகா

padaccheda.w: இறைவன் பொருள் சேர் புகழ் புரிந்தார் மாட்டு
padaccheda.m: இறைவனது மெய்ம்மை சேர்ந்த புகழை விரும்பினார் இடத்து

en.1: The two kinds of deeds, which go with darkness, do not touch those devoted to the true praise of the Lord.
en.2: Neither of the two deeds, good and bad, which come of delusion, comes to those who always speak the true praise of the Lord. Delusion is called darkness because no one can say what it is. Good deeds count too, because they also cause birth. The ignorant praise others who lack the Lord’s qualities, and that praise is empty. Only praise of him, who has them all, is true.

padaccheda.m: (மெய் வாய் கண் மூக்குச் செவி என்னும்) பொறிகளை வழியாக உடைய ஐந்து அவாவினையும் அறுத்தானது
மெய்யான ஒழுக்க நெறியின்கண் வழுவாது நின்றார்
(பிறப்பின்றி) எக்காலத்தும் (ஒருதன்மையராய்) வாழ்வார்

en.1: Those who stay on the true path of the one who quenched the five senses will live long.
en.2: The one who cut off the five desires that work through the senses of body, mouth, eyes, nose and ears taught a true path of conduct. Those who never stray from it live for all time, free of birth and unchanging. There are five desires because there are five sense objects. Couplets 3 to 6 say that those who think of the Lord, praise him and keep to his path gain release.

padaccheda.w: தனக்கு உவமை இல்லாதான் தாள் சேர்ந்தார்க்கு அல்லால்
padaccheda.m: (ஒருவாற்றானும்) தனக்கு நிகர்இல்லாதவனது, தாளைச் சேர்ந்தார்க்கல்லது
மனத்தின்கண் நிகழும் துன்பங்களை நீக்குதல் உண்டாகாது

en.1: Unless you reach the feet of the one who has no equal, the sorrow in your mind is hard to remove.
en.2: Only those who reach the feet of the one without equal in any way can remove the sorrows of the mind. “Hard” here means it can’t be done. Those who don’t reach his feet can’t end the desire, anger and delusion that cause birth, so they are born and die and sink in the suffering these bring.

padaccheda.w: அறம் ஆழி அந்தணன் தாள் சேர்ந்தார்க்கு அல்லால்
padaccheda.m: அறக் கடலாகிய அந்தணனது, தாளாகிய புணையைச் சேர்ந்தார்க்கல்லது
(அதனிற்) பிறவாகிய கடல்களை நீந்தல் அரிது

en.1: Unless you reach the feet of the sage who is a sea of righteousness, the other seas are hard to swim.
en.2: Only those who reach the raft of the feet of the sage who is a sea of righteousness can swim the other seas, which are wealth and pleasure. All kinds of righteousness make up his form, so he is called a sea of it. Those who don’t reach that raft see no shore and sink. Some read the sea as a wheel of righteousness.

reading.note: பிறவாழி can also be taken as the sea of births, as in K10. He takes it as “other seas”, meaning wealth and pleasure.

padaccheda.m: (தத்தமக்கு ஏற்ற புலன்களைக்) கொள்கையில்லாத பொறிகள் போலப் பயன் படுதலை உடையவல்ல
எண்வகைப்பட்ட குணங்களை உடையானது தாள்களை வணங்காத தலைகள்

en.1: A head that won’t bow at the feet of the one with eight qualities is as useless as a sense that senses nothing.
en.2: Heads that don’t bow to the feet of the one with eight qualities are as useless as senses that can’t take in their objects. The Saiva scriptures list the eight: independence, a pure body, natural understanding, knowing all, natural freedom from bonds, great compassion, endless power and boundless joy. Tongues that don’t praise him are just as useless.

padaccheda.m: இறைவன் அடி என்னும் புணையைச் (சேர்ந்தார்), பிறவியாகிய பெரிய கடலை நீந்துவர்
(அதனைச்) சேராதார், நீந்தமாட்டாராய் (அதனுள்) அழுந்துவர்

en.1: Those who reach the Lord’s feet swim the great sea of births. Those who do not reach them will not.
en.2: Those who reach the raft of the Lord’s feet swim the great sea of birth. Those who don’t can’t swim and sink in it. Those who think only of his feet and not of the world’s ways have their births ended, and those who think otherwise don’t.

padaccheda.m: மழை இடையறாது நிற்ப உலகம் நிலைபெற்று வருதலான்
அம்மழைதான் (உலகத்திற்கு) அமிழ்தம் என்று உணரும் பான்மையை உடையது

en.1: Because the rain keeps coming, the world keeps going. So rain should be known as ambrosia.
en.2: Because rain goes on without a break, the world endures, so rain is to be understood as the world’s ambrosia. “World” means living beings, who endure by being born without end, always seen in bodies. Those who take ambrosia don’t die, so the rain that keeps the world enduring is to be known by that name.

padaccheda.m: உண்பார்க்கு நல்ல உணவுகளை உளவாக்கி
(அவற்றை) உண்கின்றார்க்குத் தானும் உணவாய் நிற்பதூஉம் மழை

en.1: Rain makes good food for those who eat, and rain is itself food for them too.
en.2: Rain produces good foods for those who eat, and for those eating them it is food itself, because it is drunk as water. This is said of people but holds for other creatures too. By ending hunger and thirst in this way, rain keeps living beings going.

padaccheda.m: மழை வேண்டுங் காலத்துப் பெய்யாது பொய்க்குமாயின்
கடலாற் சூழப்பட்ட அகன்ற உலகத்தின்கண்
நிலைபெற்று (உயிர்களை) வருத்தும் பசி

en.1: If the sky fails, hunger will settle in the wide world of spreading waters and torment it.
en.2: If rain fails when it is needed, hunger settles in the wide world ringed by the sea and afflicts living beings. The sea is mentioned because, though the world has it, it is no help. With no food, beings die of hunger.

padaccheda.m: உழவர் ஏரான் உழுதலைச் செய்யார்
மழை என்னும் வருவாய் (தன்) பயன் குன்றின்

en.1: If the riches called rain run short, farmers will not plough.
en.2: Farmers do no ploughing if the income called rain falls short. This gives the reason why food runs out.

padaccheda.m: (பூமியின்கண் வாழ்வாரைப் பெய்யாது நின்று) கெடுப்பதூஉம்
(அவ்வாறு) கெட்டார்க்குத் துணையாய்(ப் பெய்து) முன் கெடுத்தாற்போல எடுப்பதூஉம்
இவை எல்லாம் (வல்லது) மழை

en.1: It is rain that ruins, and rain again that stands by the ruined and lifts them up. All of it is rain.
en.2: By not falling, rain ruins those who live on the earth. Then, by falling, it helps the ruined and raises them as it ruined them. Rain can do all of this. “All” is said because people’s efforts differ, so the ruinings and raisings are many. This tells the power of rain.

padaccheda.m: மேகத்தின் துளி வீழின் காண்பதல்லது

padaccheda.w: மற்று ஆங்கே பசும்புல் தலை காண்பு அரிது
padaccheda.m: வீழாதாயின், அப்பொழுதே பசும்புல்லினது தலையையும் காண்டல் அரிது

en.1: Unless drops fall from the sky, it is hard to see even the head of green grass.
en.2: You see it only if drops fall from the cloud. If they don’t, at that very moment it is hard to see even the tip of green grass. So not even life with one sense remains.

padaccheda.m: அளவில்லாத கடலும் தன்னியல்பு குறையும்

padaccheda.w: எழிலி தான் தடிந்து நல்காது ஆகி விடின்
padaccheda.m: மேகந்தான் (அதனைக்) குறைத்து (அதன்கட்) பெய்யாது விடுமாயின்

en.1: Even the vast sea would lose its nature, if the clouds took from it and gave nothing back.
en.2: Even the boundless sea loses its nature if the cloud draws from it and doesn’t rain back into it. Losing its nature means that sea creatures aren’t born and gems and the like don’t form. Even the sea, the source of rain, needs rain. These seven couplets say rain is what keeps the world going.

padaccheda.m: தேவர்கட்கும் இவ்வுலகில் (மக்களாற் செய்யப்படும்) விழவோடு கூடிய பூசையும் நடவாது
மழை பெய்யாதாயின்

en.1: If the sky dries up, festivals and worship will cease here, even for the gods.
en.2: If rain doesn’t fall, even the gods get no worship from people in this world, neither the daily rite nor the festival joined to it. The festival is performed to make up for lapses in the daily rite, so it is named first.

padaccheda.w: வியன் உலகம் தானம் தவம் இரண்டும் தங்கா
padaccheda.m: அகன்ற உலகின்கண் தானமும் தவமும் ஆகிய இரண்டு அறமும் உளவாகா
மழை பெய்யாதாயின்

en.1: If the sky does not give, neither giving nor austerity will remain in the wide world.
en.2: If rain doesn’t fall, the two righteous acts of giving and austerity don’t exist in the wide world. Giving means handing rightly earned wealth to the worthy, gladly. Austerity means cutting down food through vows, so that the mind doesn’t run after the senses. Giving belongs mostly to household life and austerity to renunciation.

padaccheda.w: யார்யார்க்கும் நீர் இன்று உலகு அமையாது எனின்
padaccheda.m: எவ்வகை மேம்பட்டார்க்கும் நீரையின்றி உலகியல் அமையாதாயின்
(அந்நீர் இடையறாது ஒழுகும்) ஒழுக்கும் வானையின்றி அமையாது

en.1: If the world can’t go on without water, then for everyone, conduct can’t go on without rain.
en.2: For people of any rank, worldly life, meaning wealth and pleasure, can’t go on without water. In the same way the unbroken flow of that water can’t go on without rain. Everyone accepts the first, so the second is clear. Some read it that without rain no one’s conduct is complete. These three couplets say rain keeps righteousness, wealth and pleasure going.

reading.note: ஒழுக்கு can mean conduct or flow. The plain reading takes conduct. He takes the flow of water, and joins “everyone” to the first half.

padaccheda.m: (தமக்குரிய) ஒழுக்கத்தின் கண்ணே (நின்று) துறந்தாரது பெருமையை
விழுமிய பொருள்கள் பலவற்றுள்ளும் (இதுவே விழுமிது என) விளம்பும், நூல்களது துணிவு

en.1: The settled view of the books is that the greatness of those who renounce while holding to right conduct stands above all else.
en.2: The books settle that, of all excellent things, the greatness of those who renounce while keeping their own conduct is highest. Keeping the conduct of your varna and stage of life grows righteousness, wears down sin and ends ignorance. Longing for release, yoga and true knowledge follow, and “mine” and “I” fall away. Even religious books that disagree agree on this.

padaccheda.m: (இருவகைப் பற்றினையும்) விட்டாரது பெருமையை இவ்வளவு என்று (எண்ணால்) கூறி அறியலுறின், (அளவுபடாமையான்)
இவ்வுலகத்துப் பிறந்து இறந்தாரை எண்ணி (இத்துணையர் என) அறியலு்ற்றாற் போலும்

en.1: Trying to measure the greatness of those who renounce is like counting all who have died on earth.
en.2: To state in a number the greatness of those who have let go of both kinds of attachment is like trying to count all who have been born in this world and died. It can’t be done.

padaccheda.m: (பிறப்பு வீடு என்னும்) இரண்டனது (துன்ப வின்பக்) கூறுபாடுகளை ஆராய்ந்து அறிந்து
(அப்பிறப்பு அறுத்தற்கு) இப்பிறப்பின்கண் துறவறத்தைப் பூண்டாரது பெருமையே
உலகின்கண் உயர்ந்தது

en.1: The greatness of those who have weighed the two and taken up righteousness here shines out in the world.
en.2: Only the greatness of those who have examined birth and release, the sorrow of one and the joy of the other, and taken up the righteousness of renunciation here to end birth, stands high in the world. “Only” sets it above the greatness of emperors who ruled the whole earth. These three couplets say the greatness of those who renounce exceeds all other greatness.

reading.note: “The two” is all the Tamil says. He takes them as birth and release, and the righteousness as renunciation.

padaccheda.m: திண்மை என்னும் தோட்டியால், (பொறிகளாகிய யானை) ஐந்தனையும் (தத்தம் புலன்கள்மேற் செல்லாமற்) காப்பான்
(எல்லா நிலத்தினும்) மிக்கது என்று சொல்லப்படும் வீட்டுநிலத்திற்கு ஓர் வித்தாம்

en.1: Whoever guards the five senses with the goad called firmness is a seed for the land called the highest.
en.2: Whoever uses the goad of firmness to hold the five elephants of the senses back from their objects is a seed for the land of release, called the highest of all lands. Firmness here means knowledge. He is called a seed because he sprouts in that land: he isn’t someone who is born here and dies and comes back.

padaccheda.m: (புலன்களிற் செல்கின்ற) அவா ஐந்தனையும் அடக்கினானது வலிக்கு

padaccheda.w: அகல் விசும்புளார் கோமான் இந்திரனே சாலும் கரி
padaccheda.m: அகன்ற வானத்துள்ளார் இறைவனாகிய இந்திரனே அமையுஞ் சான்று

en.1: Of the strength of one who quenched the five senses, Indra himself, ruler of those in the wide sky, is witness enough.
en.2: Indra, ruler of those in the wide sky, is witness enough to the strength of one who has held down all five desires. He didn’t quench them himself and fell under a curse, and that shows the strength of one who did.

padaccheda.m: (ஒத்த பிறப்பினாராய மக்களுள்) செய்தற்கு (எளியவற்றைச் செய்யாது) அரியவற்றைச் செய்வார் பெரியர்
(அவ்வெளியவற்றைச் செய்து) அரியவற்றைச் செய்யமாட்டாதார் சிறியர்

en.1: Those who do what is hard to do are great. Those who can’t are small.
en.2: Among people of equal birth, those who leave what is easy and do what is hard are great. Those who do the easy and can’t do the hard are small. The easy is letting the mind run to sense objects, with greed and anger. The hard is the eight limbs of yoga. He rejects taking it as ascetic feats like bathing often, which fall within one limb and don’t suit this greatness.

padaccheda.w: சுவை ஒளி ஊறு ஓசை நாற்றம் என்ற ஐந்தின் வகை
padaccheda.m: சுவையும் ஒளியும் ஊறும் ஓசையும் நாற்றமும் என்று சொல்லப்பட்ட (தன்மாத்திரைகள்) ஐந்தனது கூறுபாட்டையும்
ஆராய்வான் கண்ணதே உலகம்

en.1: The world lies with the one who knows the workings of the five: taste, light, touch, sound and smell.
en.2: The world lies within the understanding of one who examines the divisions of these five subtle elements. With the gross elements and the organs of sense and action they make twenty. The self, intellect, ego, mind and root nature make twenty-five, as Samkhya teaches. No world exists apart from these. The causes of greatness are quenching the five, yoga and true knowledge.

padaccheda.m: நிறைந்த மொழியினை உடைய துறந்தாரது பெருமையை
நிலவுலகத்தின் கண் (அவர் ஆணையாகச் சொல்லிய) மந்திரங்களே (கண்கூடாகக்) காட்டும்

en.1: The hidden words of people whose speech comes true show their greatness on earth.
en.2: The mantras they speak as commands show, before your eyes, the greatness on earth of those who have renounced, whose words are full. A full word gives its result whether spoken in compassion or in anger. To show here means to make known through the result.

padaccheda.w: குணம் என்னும் குன்று ஏறி நின்றார் வெகுளி
padaccheda.m: (துறவு மெய்யுணர்வு அவாவின்மை முதலிய) நற்குணங்களாகிய குன்றின் முடிவின்கண் நின்ற முனிவரது வெகுளி
(தான் உள்ளவளவு) கணமேயாயினும், (வெகுளப்பட்டாரால்) தடுத்தல் அரிது

en.1: The anger of those who stand on the hill called virtue is hard to withstand, even for a moment.
en.2: The anger of ascetics who stand at the top of the hill of good qualities, such as renunciation, true knowledge and freedom from craving, is hard for its target to stop, even for the instant it lasts. Qualities are a hill because they are firm and great. Old habit may raise anger, but true knowledge destroys it at once. It can’t be stopped because their word is full.

padaccheda.m: எல்லா உயிர்கள்மேலும் செவ்விய தண்ணளியைப் பூண்டு ஒழுகலான்
அந்தணர் என்று சொல்லப்படுவார் துறவறத்தின் நின்றவர்

en.1: Those called sages are the righteous, because they live with tenderness towards every living thing.
en.2: Those called sages are those in the righteousness of renunciation, because they take a vow of fine tenderness towards all living beings. The name means people of lovely coolness, so it applies only to those with such compassion. Though they have the power of command, they have compassion for all beings.

padaccheda.m: வீடு பேற்றையும் தரும்
(துறக்கம் முதலிய) செல்வத்தையும் தரும்: உயிர்க்கு அறத்தின் ஊஉங்கு ஆக்கம் எவன்ஓ = ஆதலான் உயிர்கட்கு அறத்தின்மிக்க ஆக்கம் யாது?

en.1: Righteousness brings distinction and it brings wealth. What gain could be greater for a living being?
en.2: It gives release, and it gives wealth such as heaven. So what gain is greater than righteousness? Release is called distinction because it is the best of all attainments. “Living being” here means human life, since only that can reach these two. No good is greater than righteousness.

reading.note: சிறப்பு is literally distinction. He reads it as release, and wealth as heaven and the like.

padaccheda.m: (ஒருவனுக்கு) அறம் செய்தலின் மேற்பட்ட ஆக்கமும் இல்லை
அதனை (மயக்கத்தான்) மறத்தலின் மேற்பட்ட கேடும் இல்லை

en.1: There is no gain greater than righteousness, and no ruin greater than forgetting it.
en.2: There is no gain greater than doing righteousness, and no ruin greater than forgetting it through delusion. The first half repeats the last couplet so as to say what ruin follows when it isn’t done.

padaccheda.m: (தத்தமக்கியலுந்) திறத்தான்

padaccheda.w: அறவினை ஓவாது ஏ செல்லும் வாய் எல்லாம் செயல்
padaccheda.m: அறமாகிய நல்வினையை ஒழியாதே (அஃது) எய்தும் இடத்தான்எல்லாம் செய்க

en.1: However you can, never stopping, do righteous deeds everywhere they can be done.
en.2: By whatever means you have, do righteous deeds without a break, through every channel open to them. Household righteousness is done as your wealth allows, and ascetic righteousness as your body allows. The channels are mind, speech and body, and their deeds are good thoughts, good words and good acts.

padaccheda.m: (அவ்வாற்றான் அறஞ்செய்வான்) (தன்) மனத்தின்கட் குற்றம் உடையனல்லனாக
அவ்வளவே அறமாவது
அஃதொழிந்த சொல்லும் வேடமும் (அறமெனப்படா,) ஆரவார நீர்மைய

en.1: To be without stain in your mind is all of righteousness. Everything else is noise.
en.2: Be free of fault in your mind: that much alone is righteousness. The fault is thinking evil. Words and outward show aren’t righteousness but noise, done so that others will notice. If the mind is stained, what is done by speech and body brings nothing.

padaccheda.m: (பிறர் ஆக்கம்) பொறாமையும்
(புலன்கண்மேற் செல்கின்ற) அவாவும்
(அவை ஏதுவாகப் பிறர்பால் வரும்) வெகுளியும்
(அதுபற்றி வரும்) கடுஞ்சொல்லும் (ஆகிய)
இந்நான்கினையும் கடிந்து இடையறாது நடந்தது அறமாவது

en.1: Envy, craving, anger and harsh words: righteousness is a life free of these four.
en.2: Envy of what others gain, craving for the objects of the senses, the anger towards others that these cause and the harsh words that anger brings: righteousness is what goes on without a break, free of these four. Whatever is mixed with them isn’t righteousness. This couplet and the last tell its nature.

padaccheda.m: (யாம் இதுபொழுது இளையம் ஆகலின்) இறக்குஞான்று செய்தும்எனக் கருதாது, அறத்தினை (நாள் தோறுஞ்) செய்க
அவ்வாறு செய்த அறம், (இவ்வுடம்பினின்றும் உயிர்) போங்காலத்து (அதற்கு) அழிவில்லாத துணையாம்

en.1: Don’t say “I’ll see to it some other day.” Practise righteousness, for it is the companion that doesn’t die when you die.
en.2: Don’t think “I am young, and I will do it when I am dying.” Practise righteousness daily. When life leaves this body it is the undying companion, because it stays with the soul and goes on into the next body. So do it while this passing body lasts.

padaccheda.m: அறத்தின் பயன் இதுவென்று (யாம் ஆகமவளவையான்) உணர்த்தல் வேண்டா
சிவிகையைக் காவுவானோடு செலுத்துவானிடை(க் காட்சியளவை தன்னானே உணரப்படும்)

en.1: You needn’t be told what the way of righteousness is. See it between the one who bears the palanquin and the one who rides in it.
en.2: The fruit of righteousness needn’t be taught from scripture. You can see it for yourself between the one who carries the palanquin and the one who rides in it. This is proof by sight, and it makes clear that righteousness is the undying companion.

reading.note: The Tamil can also mean: don’t say that the gap between carrier and rider is the way of righteousness. He takes it as the plain reading does, except that he reads ஆறு as fruit, not way.

padaccheda.m: (செய்யாது) கழியும் நாள் உளவாகாமல் ஒருவன் அறத்தைச் செய்யுமாயின்

padaccheda.w: அஃது ஒருவன் வாழ் நாள் வழி அடைக்கும் கல்
padaccheda.m: அச்செயல் (அவன் யாக்கையோடு) கூடுநாள் வரும் வழியை (வாராமல்) அடைக்கும் கல்லாம்

en.1: If you do good and let no day fall away, that is a stone that blocks the road of your living days.
en.2: If you do good and let no day pass idle, that deed is the stone that blocks the road by which days joined to a body come. While the two kinds of deeds born of the five faults remain, the soul stays in a body to taste their fruits, pleasure and pain. All those days are “living days”. So righteousness brings release.

padaccheda.m: இல்லறத்தோடு பொருந்தி வருவதே இன்பமாவது
அதனோடு பொருந்தாது வருவனவெல்லாம் (இன்பமாயினுந்) துன்பத்தினிடத்த
(அதுவேயுமன்றிப்) புகழும் உடையனவல்ல

en.1: Only what comes from righteousness is joy. All else is outside it, and brings no praise.
en.2: Only what comes with household righteousness is pleasure, meaning the enjoyment of desire. What comes without it, even if it is pleasure, belongs with pain, and has no praise either. Sins such as wanting another man’s wife seem pleasant for a moment and then turn to pain. Only those who do righteousness gain joy in this life, and praise.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்குச் செய்தற் பான்மையது நல்வினையே
ஒழிதற்பான்மையது, தீவினையே

en.1: What you ought to do is righteousness. What you ought to avoid is whatever brings blame.
en.2: What a person should do is good deeds. What a person should give up is evil deeds. Blame here stands for what is blamed. This lays down what to do and what to leave undone.

padaccheda.m: இல்லறத்தோடு கூடி வாழ்வானென்று சொல்லப்படுவான்
அறவியல்பினையுடைய ஏனை மூவர்க்கும், (அவர் செல்லும்) நல்லொழுக்க நெறிக்கண் நிலைபெற்ற துணையாம்

en.1: The one called a householder is a steady support on the good path for the three who live as they should.
en.2: The one called a householder, who lives in household righteousness, is a firm support on their good path to the other three: the student under vows with a teacher, the forest-dweller doing penance with his wife serving him, and the full renunciant. He gives them food, medicine and shelter, so that hunger, illness and cold don’t stop them.

reading.note: The Tamil says only “the three”. He takes them as the other stages of life.

padaccheda.m: (களைகண் 1 ஆனவரால்) துறக்கப்பட்டார்க்கும்
நல்கூர்ந்தார்க்கும்
(ஒருவருமின்றித் தன்பால் வந்து) இறந்தார்க்கும்
இல்வாழ்வானென்று சொல்லப்படுவான் துணை

en.1: The one called a householder is the support of those who have renounced, those who have nothing, and the dead.
en.2: The one called a householder is a support to those forsaken by their protectors, to the poor, and to those who come to him with no one and die. He stands as protector to the forsaken, so that they stay free of sin, and does what they need. He gives the poor food and more. For the dead he does water rites and the like, and sends them to a good world.

reading.note: துறந்தார் normally means those who have renounced, as in chapter 3. He reads it as those forsaken by their protectors.

padaccheda.w: தென்புலத்தார் தெய்வம் விருந்து ஒக்கல் தான் என்ற
padaccheda.m: பிதிரர் தேவர் விருந்தினர் சுற்றத்தார் தான் என்று சொல்லப்பட்ட
ஐந்திடத்துஞ் செய்யும் அறநெறியை வழுவாமற் செய்தல் (இல்வாழ்வானுக்குச்) சிறப்புடைய அறமாம்

en.1: The ancestors in the south, the gods, guests, kin and yourself: looking after these five is the chief duty.
en.2: Keeping the righteous ways towards ancestors, gods, guests, kin and yourself is the householder’s chief righteousness. The ancestors are a class of god made by Brahma at creation, and their place is the south. Guests are new arrivals, expected or not. You count because righteousness needs you alive to do it. So a ruler’s tax is one sixth: five shares go to these.

padaccheda.m: (பொருள் செய்யுங்கால்) பாவத்தை யஞ்சி (யீட்டி), பாத்து = (அப்பொருளை இயல்புடைய மூவர் முதலாயினார்க்கும், தென்புலத்தார் முதலிய நால்வர்க்கும்) பகுத்து, ஊண் = (தான்) உண்டலை, வாழ்க்கை = (ஒருவன்) இல் வாழ்க்கை, உடைத்து ஆயின் = உடைத்தாயின், வழி = அவன் வழி (உலகத்து), எஞ்ஞான்றும் = எஞ்ஞான்றும், எஞ்சல் இல் = (நிற்றலல்லது) இறத்தலில்லை

en.1: If your life fears blame and shares its food, your line will never die out.
en.2: If you fear sin while earning wealth, and share it with those named above before you eat, your line never dies out in the world. If you share another’s wealth gained by sin, the merit goes to its owner, the sin stays with you and your line ends. That is why he says to fear blame.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவன் இல்வாழ்க்கை, அன்பும் = (தன் துணைவிமேற் செய்யத்தகும்) அன்பினையும், அறனும் = (பிறர்க்குப் பகுத்துண்டலாகிய) அறத்தினையும், உடைத்து ஆயின் = உடைத்தாயின்
அவ்வுடைமை, பண்பும் பயனும் = (அதற்குப்) பண்பும் பயனுமாம்

en.1: If home life has loving-kindness and righteousness, that is its quality and its fruit.
en.2: If your home life has loving-kindness towards your wife and the righteousness of sharing with others, these are its quality and its fruit, in that order. Household righteousness can’t last unless wife and husband are of one heart, so loving-kindness is the quality and righteousness the fruit.

padaccheda.m: (ஒருவன்) இல்வாழ்க்கையை அறத்தின் வழியே செலுத்துவானாயின்
(அவன்) அதற்குப் புறமாகிய நெறியிற் போய்ப் பெறும் பயன் யாது?

en.1: If you live your home life in the way of righteousness, what would you gain by going off on some outside path?
en.2: If you lead home life by the path of righteousness, what more can you gain by going down the path outside it? That path of righteousness is fearing blame, sharing food and having loving-kindness. The outside path is leaving home for the forest. Home life brings more than that stage does.

padaccheda.m: இல்வாழ்க்கைக்கண் நின்று (அதற்குரிய) இயல்போடு கூடி வாழ்பவனென்று சொல்லப்படுவான்
(புலன்களைவிட) முயல்வார் எல்லாருள்ளும் மிக்கவன்

en.1: The one who lives home life as it should be lived is first among all who strive.
en.2: The one who lives home life with its proper nature is above all those who strive to give up the senses. “Those who strive” are those in the third stage of life, since those who have fully renounced have already let go. That stage has many forms, so he says “all”. The householder comes first because he gets the fruit without such striving.

padaccheda.m: (தவஞ்செய்வாரையுந் தத்தம்) நெறிக்கண் ஒழுகப்பண்ணித் (தானுந் தன்) அறத்திற் றவறாத இல்வாழ்க்கை
அத்தவஞ்செய்வார் நிலையினும் பொறை யுடைத்து

en.1: A home life that keeps others on their path and doesn’t slip from righteousness has more endurance than those who do penance.
en.2: A home life that keeps ascetics going on their own paths, and doesn’t itself slip from righteousness, has more endurance than those ascetics. It takes away obstacles such as hunger. Ascetics bear only the pain that falls on them, while householders also bear the pain of others.

padaccheda.m: (இருவகையறத்தினும் நூல்களான்) அறனென்று சிறப்பித்துச் சொல்லப்பட்டது, இல்வாழ்க்கையே
(ஏனைத் துறவறமோவெனின்) அதுவும், பிறனாற் பழிக்கப்படுவதில்லைஆயின், (அவ்வில்வாழ்க்கையோடு ஒரு தன்மைத்தாக) நன்று

en.1: What is called righteousness is home life, and it too is good if no one else can blame it.
en.2: Of the two kinds of righteousness, the books name home life alone as righteousness. Renunciation too is good, like home life, if others can’t blame it for false conduct. It is hard, punishing mind and senses, while home life easily enjoys the five senses to the full, yet it is counted with home life only when it is that hard.

reading.note: “It too” points back to home life in the plain reading. He points it at renunciation: that too is good, if it isn’t blamed.

padaccheda.m: (இல்லறத்தோடு கூடி) வாழும் இயல்பினால், வையத்தின்கண் வாழ்பவன்
(வையத்தானே யெனினும்) வானின்கண் உறையுந் தேவருள் ஒருவனாக வைத்து நன்கு மதிக்கப்படும்

en.1: One who lives in this world as a life should be lived will be counted among the gods who dwell in the sky.
en.2: One who lives on earth in the way of home life is honoured as one of the gods who dwell in the sky, though still on earth. He is sure to become a god later and enjoy the fruit of this righteousness. This tells the reward of home life in the next world. Its reward in this world is fame, told later.

padaccheda.w: மனைத் தக்க மாண்பு உடையளாகித் தன் கொண்டான் வளம் தக்காள்
padaccheda.m: மனையறத்திற்குத் தக்க, நற்குண நற்செய்கைகளை யுடையளாய்த் தன்னைக் கொண்டவனது வருவாய்க்குத் தக்க வாழ்க்கையை யுடையாள்
அதற்குத் துணை

en.1: She is a life’s companion who has the worth a home needs and lives within the means of the man who took her.
en.2: She is a companion to home life who has the good qualities and deeds household righteousness needs, and lives within the income of the man who took her. The qualities are caring for ascetics, feeding guests and compassion for the poor. The deeds are knowing and keeping what the home needs, skill in the kitchen and doing what is fitting.

padaccheda.m: மனையறத்திற்குத் தக்க நற்குண நற்செய்கைகள், (ஒருவன்) இல்லாளிடத்து இல்லையாயின்
அவ்வில்வாழ்க்கை, (செல்வத்தான்) எத்துணை மாட்சிமைத்தாயினும் (அஃது) உடைத்தன்று

en.1: If a wife lacks the worth a home needs, that life is nothing, however fine it may be.
en.2: If a wife lacks the good qualities and deeds that household righteousness needs, that home life has nothing, however splendid it is with wealth. It is called nothing because it is of no use.

padaccheda.m: (ஒருவனுக்கு) இல்லாள், நற்குண நற்செய்கையள் ஆயினக்கால் இல்லாதது யாது? இல்லவள் மாணாக் கடை உள்ளது என் = அவள் அன்னளல்லாக்கால் உள்ளது யாது?

en.1: What is lacking if the wife has worth? What is there if she has none?
en.2: If a man’s wife has good qualities and deeds, what does he lack? If she doesn’t, what does he have? These two couplets say that what home life needs is the worth of the wife and nothing else.

padaccheda.m: (ஒருவனெய்தும் பொருள்களுள்) இல்லாளின் மேம்பட்ட பொருள்கள் யாவையுள
(அவள்மாட்டுக்) கற்பு என்னும் கலங்காநிலைமை யுண்டாகப்பெறின்?

en.1: What is greater than a woman, if she has the strength called chastity?
en.2: Of all a man can gain, what is greater than a wife, if she has the unshaken state called chastity? Nothing else serves as a chaste woman does as the cause of righteousness, wealth and pleasure. This tells the excellence of chastity.

padaccheda.w: தெய்வம் தொழாஅள் கொழுநன் தொழுது எழுவாள் பெய் என
padaccheda.m: (பிற) தெய்வந் தொழாது (தன்தெய்வமாகிய) கொழுநனைத் தொழாநின்று துயிலெழுவாள் பெய்யென்று சொல்ல
மழை பெய்யும்

en.1: A woman who worships no god but wakes worshipping her husband has only to say “Rain”, and it rains.
en.2: She worships no other god and rises from sleep worshipping her husband, who is her god. If she says “Rain”, it rains. The mind is clearest for worship on waking, so he speaks of rising. The god itself obeys her. This tells the power of a chaste woman.

padaccheda.m: (கற்பினின்றும் வழுவாமல்) தன்னைக் காத்துத், தன்னைக் கொண்டவனையும் (உண்டி முதலியவற்றால்) பேணி
(இருவர் மாட்டும்) நன்மையமைந்த புகழ் நீங்காமற் காத்து
(மேற்சொல்லிய நற்குண நற்செய்கைகளினுங்) கடைப்பிடியுடையாளே பெண்ணாவாள்

en.1: A woman is one who guards herself, cares for the man who took her, guards their good name and never flags.
en.2: A true woman guards herself so as not to slip from chastity, tends the man who took her with food and the like, keeps the good fame of both from leaving them, and holds firm to the good qualities and deeds named above. Her own fame is the praise of her chastity in the town where she lives. Flagging means forgetting.

padaccheda.w: மகளிர் சிறை காக்கும் காப்பு எவன் செய்யும்
padaccheda.m: மகளிரைத் தலைவர் சிறையாற் காக்குங் காவல் என்னபயனைச் செய்யும்? நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பே தலை = அவர் (தமது) நிறையாற் காக்கும் காவலே தலையாய காவல்

en.1: What use is guarding women behind walls? The best guard is the one they keep by their own restraint.
en.2: What good does it do men to guard women by confinement, with walls and gatekeepers? The guard they keep by their own restraint, holding the heart to chastity, is the chief guard. Without it, confinement is useless.

padaccheda.m: பெண்டிர், (தம்மை) எய்திய கணவனை (வழிபடுதல்) பெறுவராயின்
புத்தேளிர் வாழுமுலகின்கண் (அவராற்) பெருஞ்சிறப்பினைப் பெறுவர்

en.1: If women gain the man who gained them, they gain great honour in the world where the gods live.
en.2: If women have the husband who took them, and worship him, they receive great honour from the gods in the world where the gods live. Women who tend the man who took them are tended by the gods.

reading.note: The first words are compressed: “if they gain the one who gained them”. He supplies worship of the husband.

padaccheda.m: புகழை விரும்பிய இல்லாளை யில்லாதார்க்கு

padaccheda.w: இகழ்வார் முன் ஏறுபோல் பீடு நடை இல்லை
padaccheda.m: (தம்மை) இகழ்ந்துரைக்கும் பகைவர்முன் சிங்கவேறு போல நடக்கும் பெருமிதநடை இல்லை

en.1: Those without a wife who cares for a good name can’t walk proud as a bull before those who scorn them.
en.2: Those who have no wife who loves fame don’t have the proud walk of a lion before the enemies who scorn them. A lion’s walk is the figure for a man of pride. This tells the fault that follows when the wife doesn’t guard their good name.

reading.note: ஏறு is any male beast and usually a bull. He takes it as a lion.

padaccheda.m: (ஒருவற்கு) நன்மையென்று சொல்லுவர் (அறிந்தோர்), மனையாளது நற்குண நற்செய்கைகளை
அவைதமக்கு நல்ல அணிகலமென்று சொல்லுவர் நல்ல புதல்வரைப் பெறுதலை

en.1: They call the excellence of a home a blessing, and having good children its fine ornament.
en.2: The wise say a wife’s good qualities and deeds are a man’s blessing, and that gaining good sons is their fine ornament. By naming an ornament for the wife, this opens the way to the next chapter.

padaccheda.m: (ஒருவன்) பெறும் பேறுகளுள்

padaccheda.w: அறிவு அறிந்த மக்கள் பேறு அல்ல பிற
padaccheda.m: அறிய வேண்டுவன அறிதற்கு உரிய மக்களைப் பெறுதலல்லது பிறபேறுகளை
யாம் மதிப்பதில்லை

en.1: Of all that can be gained, we know of nothing else like children with understanding.
en.2: Among all a man can gain, we value no gain but sons fit to know what should be known. “With understanding” shows that the word for children here leaves out daughters. The past tense is used because a fit nature is sure to bring knowledge. This tells the excellence of having sons.

padaccheda.m: (வினைவயத்தாற் பிறக்கும்) பிறப்பு ஏழின் கண்ணும் (ஒருவனைத்) துன்பங்கள் சென்றடையா
(பிறரால்) பழிக்கப்படாத நற்குணங்களையுடைய புதல்வரைப் பெறுவானாயின்

en.1: In all seven births, evils won’t touch you if you have children of good character, free of blame.
en.2: In all seven births that deeds bring, suffering won’t reach a man who has sons of good qualities that no one blames. His bad deeds wear away through the gifts and righteous acts such sons perform for their parents, and their good qualities are the cause of those acts. The seven births are the seven kinds of being.

padaccheda.m: தம்புதல்வரைத் தம்பொருளென்று சொல்லுவர் (அறிந்தோர்)(
அப்புதல்வர் செய்தபொருள் தம்மை நோக்கி (அவர்) செய்யும் நல்வினையானே (தம்பால்) வரும் (ஆதலான்)

en.1: People say their children are their wealth. That wealth comes by each one’s own deeds.
en.2: The wise call a man’s sons his wealth, because what those sons earn comes to him through the good deeds they do for his sake. Sons who earn are called wealth as a manner of speaking. These two couplets tell the reward of good sons in the next life.

padaccheda.m: (சுவையான்) அமிழ்தத்தினும் மிக வினிமை யுடைத்து
தம் மக்களது சிறுகையான் அளாவப்பட்ட சோறு

en.1: Sweeter by far than ambrosia is the porridge your own children have stirred with their small hands.
en.2: Rice mixed by the small hands of your own children tastes far sweeter than ambrosia. To mix it is to drop it, touch it, bite it, stir it and scatter the ghee-soaked food over themselves.

padaccheda.m: (ஒருவன்) மெய்க்கு இன்பமாவது மக்களது மெய்யைத் தீண்டுதல்
செவிக்கின்பமாவது அவரது சொல்லைக் கேட்டல்

en.1: Touching your children’s bodies is joy to the body, and hearing their words is joy to the ear.
en.2: The body’s joy is touching your children’s bodies, and the ear’s joy is hearing their words. “Words” is left general because what they say once they are learned is a joy too, not only their baby talk.

padaccheda.m: குழலிசை யினிது யாழிசை யினிது என்று சொல்லுவர்
தம் புதல்வருடைய குதலைச் சொற்களைக் கேளாதவர்

en.1: “The flute is sweet, the harp is sweet,” say those who have not heard the babble of their own children.
en.2: Those who haven’t heard the lisping words of their own sons say the music of the flute and the harp is sweet. Those who have heard them would call those words sweeter. These three couplets tell the reward of children in this life.

padaccheda.m: தந்தை புதல்வனுக்குச் செய்யும் நன்மையாவது
(கற்றார்) அவையத்தின்கண் (அவரினும்) மிக்கிருக்குமாறு கல்வியுடையனாக்குதல். பொருளுடையனாக்குதல் முதலாயின, துன்பம் பயத்தலின் நன்மையாகாவென்பது கருத்து. இதனால் தந்தை கடன் & கூறப்பட்டது. (&. கடன்= கடமை)

en.1: The good a father does his son is to put him in the front rank of the assembly.
en.2: The good a father does his son is to make him so learned that he stands above others in the assembly of the learned. Making him rich and the like isn’t good, because that brings suffering. This tells the father’s duty.

padaccheda.m: தம் மக்களதறிவுடைமை

padaccheda.w: மா நிலத்து மன் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் தம்மின் இனிது
padaccheda.m: பெரிய நிலத்து மன்னாநின்ற உயிர்கட்கெல்லாம் தம்மினுமினிதாம்

en.1: That your children know more than you is sweet to every living being on this great earth.
en.2: Your children’s understanding is sweeter to all those on this great earth than it is to you. Understanding here means learning joined to natural intelligence. “Living beings” means the wise, since only they can delight in seeing it. So the assembly rejoices even more than the father.

reading.note: தம்மின், “than oneself”, can go with the children’s understanding, as here. He joins it to “sweet”: their understanding is sweeter to the world than to the parent.

padaccheda.m: (தான்) பெற்ற பொழுதை மகிழ்ச்சியினும் மிக மகிழும்
தன்மகனைக் (கல்வி கேள்விகளான்) நிறைந்தானென்று (அறிவுடையார்) சொல்லக் கேட்ட தாய்

en.1: A mother who hears her son called a man of worth feels more joy than when she bore him.
en.2: A mother who hears the wise call her son complete in learning rejoices more than at the time she bore him. A mother’s joy in her child has no measure, so it is told on its own here.

padaccheda.m: (கல்வியுடையனாக்கிய) தந்தைக்கு மகன் செய்யும் கைம்மாறாவது
(தன் அறிவும் ஒழுக்கமுங் கண்டார்), இவன் தந்தை (இவனைப்) பெறுதற்கு என்ன தவஞ் செய்தான்கொல்லோவென்று சொல்லுஞ் சொல்லை நிகழ்த்துதல்

en.1: What a son does in return for his father is to make people say, “What penance did his father do to have him?”
en.2: The return a son makes to the father who had him taught is to live so that people who see his understanding and conduct say, “What penance did his father do to get him?” This tells the son’s duty.

padaccheda.m: அன்பிற்கும் (பிறரறியாமல்) அடைத்து வைக்குந் தாழுளதோ? ஆர்வலர் புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும் = (தம்மாலன்பு செய்யப்பட்டாரது துன்பங்கண்டுழி) அன்புடையார்கண் பொழிகின்ற புல்லிய கண்ணீரே (உள் நின்ற அன்பினை எல்லாரும்) அறியத் தூற்றும் (ஆதலான்)

en.1: Can any lock keep loving-kindness hidden? The tears of those who have it will give it away.
en.2: Can loving-kindness be locked away so that no one knows? When people who have it see those dear to them suffer, their tears tell everyone. It can’t be seen, but it can be inferred.

padaccheda.m: அன்பிலாதார் (பிறர்க்குப் பயன்படாமையின்) எல்லாப் பொருளானுந் தமக்கே யுரியர்
அன்பு உடையார், (அவற்றானேயன்றித் தம்) உடம்பானும் பிறர்க்குரியர்

en.1: People without loving-kindness keep everything for themselves. People with it would give even their bones for others.
en.2: Those without it are of no use to others, so all they own stays theirs alone. Those who have it belong to others with their bodies too, not only with what they own. “Bones” stands for the body.

padaccheda.m: (பெறுதற்கு) அரிய மக்களுயிர்க்கு உடம்போடுண்டாகிய தொடர்ச்சியினை
அன்போடு பொருந்துதற்கு வந்த நெறியின் பயனென்று சொல்லுவர் அறிந்தோர்

en.1: They say the precious soul is joined to a body of bone so that it can practise loving-kindness.
en.2: Human life is hard to obtain. Its bond with the body exists for loving-kindness, because it can’t be practised without a body. So the purpose of being embodied is loving-kindness.

padaccheda.m: (ஒருவனுக்குத் தொடர்புடையார்மாட்டுச் செய்த) அன்பு, (அத்தன்மையாற் பிறர்மாட்டும்) விருப்பமுடைமையைத் தரும்

padaccheda.w: அது நண்பு என்னும் நாடாச் சிறப்பு ஈனும்
padaccheda.m: அவ்விருப்பமுடைமைதான் (இவற்குப் பகையும் நொதுமலுமில்லையாய்) யாவரும் நண்பு என்று சொல்லப்படும் அளவிறந்த சிறப்பினைத் தரும்

en.1: Loving-kindness makes you warm towards people, and that warmth brings friendship, a gift beyond measure.
en.2: Loving-kindness shown to your own people grows into goodwill towards others. That goodwill leaves you with no enemies and no strangers, so that everyone is your friend, and this is a distinction beyond measure.

padaccheda.m: அன்புடையராய் (இல்லறத்தோடு) பொருந்திய நெறியின் பயன் என்று சொல்லுவர் (அறிந்தோர்)
இவ்வுலகத்து (இல்வாழ்க்கைக்கணின்று) இன்பநுகர்ந்து (அதன்மேல் துறக்கத்துச் சென்று) எய்தும் பேரின்பத்தினை

en.1: They say the happiness of those who are happy in this world comes from a life settled in loving-kindness.
en.2: The reward is heaven. People who are happy in household life with wife, children and kin become gods through the sacrifices they performed, and are happy there too. Ascetics suffer to reach that heaven. Only loving-kindness lets you reach it through happiness.

reading.note: Parimelazhagar moves the reward from this world to the next.

padaccheda.m: அன்பு துணையாவது அறத்திற்கே என்று சொல்லுவர் (சிலர்), அறியார்
(ஏனை) மறத்திற்கும் அவ்வன்பே துணையாவது

en.1: Only the ignorant say loving-kindness helps righteousness alone. It helps against hostility too.
en.2: Some say loving-kindness supports righteousness only, and they are ignorant. When someone wrongs you and hostility rises in your heart, treat that person as a friend and show them loving-kindness, and the hostility goes.

reading.note: He reads the hostility as your own, not someone else’s.

padaccheda.m: என்பில்லாத வுடம்பை, வெயில் காய்ந்தாற்போலக் காயும்

அன்பில்லாதவுயிரை அறக்கடவுள். 'என்பிலது' என்றதனான் உடம்பென்பதூஉம், 'அன்பிலது' என்றதனான் உயிரென்பதூஉம் பெற்றாம். வெறுப்பின்றி எங்குமொருதன்மைத்தாகிய வெயிலின்முன், என்பில்லது தன்னியல்பாற் சென்று கெடுமாறு போல, அத்தன்மைத்தாகிய அறத்தின்முன் அன்பில்லது தன்னியல்பாற் கெடுமென்பதாம். அதனைக் 'காயு'மென வெயிலறங்களின் மேலேற்றினார், அவவற்றிற்கும் அவ்வியல்பு உண்மையின். இவ்வாறு "அல்லவை செய்தார்க் கறங்கூற்றம்" (நான்மணிக்கடிகை, 84) எனப் பிறருங் கூறினார். இக்குறள் உவமையணி

en.1: As the sun scorches a creature with no bones, righteousness scorches a person with no loving-kindness.
en.2: The god of righteousness burns the soul without loving-kindness, as the sun burns a body without bones. The sun has no malice: the boneless thing perishes before it by its own nature, and so does such a soul before righteousness.

padaccheda.m: மனத்தின்கண் அன்பி்ல்லாத உயிர் (இல்லறத்தோடு கூடி) வாழ்தல்
வன்பாலின்கண் வற்றலாகிய மரந் தளிர்த்தாற்போலும்

en.1: A life with no loving-kindness inside is like a dead tree trying to sprout on barren ground.
en.2: For someone with no loving-kindness in the heart, living a household life is like a dried tree sprouting on hard ground. It can’t happen.

padaccheda.m: யாக்கை யகத்தின்கண் (நின்று) (இல்லறத்திற்கு) உறுப்பாகிய அன்பு உடையரல்லாதார்க்கு
ஏனைப் புறத்தின்கணின்று உறுப்பாவனவெல்லாம் (அவ்வறஞ் செய்தற்கண்) என்ன உதவியைச் செய்யும்?

en.1: What use is everything on the outside to someone who lacks loving-kindness, the part within?
en.2: The outer parts of a household are place, wealth and servants. What use are they without loving-kindness, the inner part? He rejects the reading that this means eyes and other parts of the body, because that has nothing to do with household life.

padaccheda.m: அன்பு முதலாக அதன்வழி நின்ற உடம்பே, உயிர்நின்ற உடம்பாவது

padaccheda.w: அஃது இலார்க்கு உடம்பு என்பு தோல் போர்த்த
padaccheda.m: அவ்வன்பில்லாதார்க்கு (உளவான) உடம்புகள் என்பினைத் தோலாற் போர்த்தனவாம்

en.1: A living body is one that loving-kindness moves. Without it, a body is just bones wrapped in skin.
en.2: Only a body led by loving-kindness is one with life in it. The bodies of those without it are bones covered in skin, because they yield none of the righteousness of household life.

padaccheda.m: மனைவியோடும் வனத்திற் செல்லாது இல்லின்கணிருந்து பொருள்களைப் போற்றிவாழுஞ் செய்கையெல்லாம்
விருந்தினரைப்பேணி அவர்க்குபகாரஞ் செய்தற்பொருட்டு

en.1: The whole point of staying at home and keeping things up is to care for guests and do them good.
en.2: All the work of staying at home with your wife, not going to the forest, and looking after your wealth, is so that you can care for guests and help them. Without that help, staying at home and the toil of earning wealth have no use.

padaccheda.m: உண்ணப்படும் பொருள் அமிர்தமேயெனினும்
தன்னை நோக்கிவந்த விருந்து தன்னில்லின் புறத்ததாகத் தானே உண்டல்
விரும்புதன் முறைமை யுடைத்ன்று

en.1: To eat while your guest stays outside is not to be wished for, even if it is the medicine against death.
en.2: Even if what you eat is ambrosia, you shouldn’t want to eat it alone while a guest who came to you stays outside your home. It can also be read: even if some call eating once without a guest a medicine against death, leave it. These two couplets tell the excellence of caring for guests.

padaccheda.m: தன்னை நோக்கி வந்தவிருந்தை நாடோறும் புறந்தருவான தில்வாழ்க்கை
நல்குரவான் வருந்திக் கெடுதலில்லை

en.1: The life of one who cares for the guests who come each day will not suffer and fall to ruin.
en.2: The home life of one who cares every day for the guests who come to him isn’t ruined by the misery of poverty. His wealth doesn’t shrink by this but grows more and more.

padaccheda.m: திருமகள் மனமகிழ்ந்து வாழாநிற்கும்
முகமினியனாய்த் தக்கவிருந்தினரைப் பேணுவானதில்லின்கண்

en.1: With a glad heart the goddess of fortune lives in the home of one who cares for good guests with a glad face.
en.2: The goddess of fortune lives gladly in the home of one who cares for worthy guests with a pleasant face. She is glad because her wealth is going the right way. Worthy means high in knowledge and conduct. This gives the reason why his wealth grows.

padaccheda.m: முன்னே விருந்தினரை மிசைவித்துப் பின் மிக்கதனைத் தான் மிசைவானது விளைபுலத்திற்கு
வித்திடுதலும் வேண்டுமோ? வேண்டா

en.1: Need you even sow seed in the field of one who feeds guests and eats what is left?
en.2: Does the field of one who first feeds his guests and then eats what is left even need seed sown? No. It yields by itself. These three couplets tell what those who care for guests gain in this life.

padaccheda.m: தன்கட் சென்ற விருந்தைப் பேணிப் பின் செல்லக்கடவ விருந்தைப் பார்த்துத் தான் அதனோடு உண்ணவிருப்பான்
மறுபிறப்பிற் றேவனாய் வானினுள்ளார்க்கு நல்விருந்தாம்

en.1: One who looks after the guest who is leaving and watches for the guest still to come is a good guest to those in the sky.
en.2: One who has tended the guests who came, and then watches for those still to come so as to eat with them, becomes a god in his next birth and a good guest to those in the sky. A good guest means one they seldom get. This tells the reward in the next world.

padaccheda.m: விருந்தோம்பலாகிய வேள்வியின் பயன் இன்ன அளவிற்று என்பதோர் அளவுடைத்தன்று
அதற்கு அவ்விருந்தின் தகுதியளவே அளவு

en.1: There is no saying how great the fruit of the sacrifice is. It is measured by the worth of the guest.
en.2: The reward of the sacrifice of caring for guests has no fixed measure. Its only measure is the worth of the guest. It is called a sacrifice because it is one of the five great sacrifices. The amount given doesn’t decide it, since a small gift in worthy hands grows huge. This is why it brings reward in both worlds.

padaccheda.m: நிலையாப் பொருளை வருந்திக் காத்துப் பின் அதனை இழந்து இதுபொழுது யாம் பற்றுக்கோடு இலமாயினேம் என்று இரங்குவர்
அப்பொருளான் விருந்தினரையோம்பி வேள்விப் பயனையெய்தும் பொறியிலாதார்

en.1: After anxious guarding they will say “We have nothing to hold on to”: those who never took up the sacrifice of caring for guests.
en.2: Those without the good fortune to care for guests with their wealth and gain the reward of sacrifice guard that passing wealth with pain, then lose it and lament, “Now we have no support.” Even guarding wealth is hard pain, so he says they guarded it anxiously.

padaccheda.m: உடைமைக்காலத்து இன்மையாவது விருந்தோம்பலை இகழும் பேதைமை
அஃது அறிந்தார்மாட்டு உளதாகாது, பேதையர்மாட்டே உளதாம்

en.1: Poverty amid plenty is the folly of neglecting guests. It is found among fools.
en.2: Poverty in a time of plenty is the stupidity that scorns caring for guests. It isn’t found in those who know, only in fools. It loses what wealth is for and so turns having into not having. Even if the wealth stays, it is useless. These two couplets tell the fault of not caring for guests.

padaccheda.m: அனிச்சப்பூ மோந்துழியன்றிக் குழையாது
விருந்தினர் முகம் வேறுபட்டு நோக்கக் குழைவர்

en.1: The aṉiccam flower wilts when you smell it. A guest wilts when you look at them with a changed face.
en.2: The aṉiccam flower wilts only when smelled. Guests wilt when looked at with a changed face. A host needs a pleasant face from afar, sweet words as they come near and good deeds once they accept. Without the first, they wilt and leave while still far off, so guests are more delicate than the flower. A pleasant face comes first.

padaccheda.m: இன்சொலாவன

padaccheda.w: ஈரம் அளைஇப் படிறு இலவாம் செம்பொருள் கண்டார் வாய்ச்சொல்
padaccheda.m: அன்போடு கலந்து வஞ்சனையிலவாய் இருக்கின்ற அறத்தினை உணர்ந்தார் வாயிற்சொற்கள். 'ஆல்' அசைநிலை. அன்போடு கலத்தல்= அன்புடைமையை வெளிப்படுத்தல். படிறின்மை= வாய்மை. மெய்யுணர்ந்தார் நெஞ்சிற்கெல்லாம் செம்மையுடைத்தாய்த் தோன்றலின், 'செம்பொரு'ளெனப் பட்டது. இலவாஞ் சொ்ல்லென இயையும். 'வாய்' என வேண்டாது கூறினார், தீய சொற் பயிலாவென்பது அறிவித்தற்கு. இதனான் இன்சொற்கு இலக்கணங் கூறப்பட்டது

en.1: Sweet words are what come from the mouths of those who have seen the truth: steeped in tenderness and free of deceit.
en.2: Sweet words are the words from the mouths of those who know righteousness, mixed with loving-kindness and free of deceit. To mix them is to show loving-kindness, and to be free of deceit is to be true. Righteousness is called the straight thing because it seems straight to all who know the truth. “Mouths” shows they never practise evil words.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சுவந்து ஒருவற்கு வேண்டிய பொருளைக் கொடுத்தலினும் நன்று
கண்டபொழுதே முகம் இனியனாய் அதனோடு இனிய சொல்லையும் உடையனாகப் பெறின்

en.1: Better than giving with a glad heart is to have a glad face and sweet words.
en.2: Better than gladly giving someone what they need is to have a pleasant face the moment you see them, and sweet words with it. Unlike giving, this depends on you and not on wealth, yet it doesn’t come naturally except to those with righteous hearts, so it is rarer.

padaccheda.m: கண்டபொழுதே முகத்தான் விரும்பி இனிதாக நோக்கி
பின் நண்ணியவழி மனத்துடனாகிய இனிய சொற்களைச் சொல்லுதலின் கண்ணே அறம்

en.1: Righteousness lies in a glad face, a kind look and sweet words that come from the heart.
en.2: On seeing someone, welcome them with your face and look on them kindly. Then, when they come near, say sweet words from the heart. Righteousness lies in that, not in giving. These two couplets say a pleasant face with sweet words wins people over at once, and so comes first in caring for guests.

padaccheda.m: எல்லார் மாட்டும் இன்பத்தை மிகுவிக்கும் இன்சொல்லை உடையார்க்கு
துன்பத்தை மிகுவிக்கும் நல்குரவு இல்லையாம்

en.1: The poverty that brings sorrow will not come to those whose sweet words bring joy to everyone.
en.2: Poverty, which increases sorrow, won’t come to those whose sweet words increase everyone’s joy. Poverty is the senses lacking what they would enjoy. Such people have no enemies and no strangers, only friends, and so gain all wealth.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு அணியாவது தன்னால் தாழப்படுவார்கண் தாழ்ச்சி உடையனாய் எல்லார்கண்ணும் இனிய சொல்லையும் உடையனாதல்
இவை யிரண்டுமன்றி மெய்க்கணியும் பிற அணிகள் அணியாகா

en.1: Humility and sweet words are a person’s ornaments. Nothing else is.
en.2: A person’s ornament is to bow to those one should bow to and to have sweet words for all. The other ornaments worn on the body aren’t ornaments, because they don’t give such beauty. Humility is named because it goes with sweet words. These two couplets tell the reward of sweet words in this life.

padaccheda.m: பொருளாற் பிறர்க்கு நன்மை பயக்குஞ் சொற்களை மனத்தான் ஆராய்ந்து இனியவாக ஒருவன் சொல்லுமாயின்
அவனுக்குப் பாவங்கள் தேய அறம் வளரும்

en.1: If you seek out what is good and say it sweetly, wrongs will wear away and righteousness will grow.
en.2: If you weigh in your mind words whose meaning does others good, and say them sweetly, your sins wear away and righteousness grows. Sin wastes away because its enemy, righteousness, is growing and it has no footing. Even what is good isn’t righteousness if it is said harshly. This tells the reward in the next life.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு இம்மைக்கு நீதியையும் உண்டாக்கி மறுமைக்கு அறத்தையும் பயக்கும்
பொருளாற் பிறர்க்கு நன்மையைக் கொடுத்து இனிமைப் பண்பின் நீங்காத சொல்

en.1: Words that are useful and never part from courtesy give rise to fairness and bring good.
en.2: Words whose meaning does others good, and which never lose their sweetness, bring the speaker justice in this life and righteousness in the next. Justice means being in accord with the world. Courtesy here means sweetness.

padaccheda.m: பொருளாற் பிறர்க்கு நோய் செய்யாத இனிய சொல்
ஒருவனுக்கு இருமையினும் இன்பத்தைப் பயக்கும்

en.1: Sweet words free of all meanness bring joy in the next life and in this one.
en.2: Sweet words that cause others no pain by their meaning give you joy in both worlds. The next life is named first because its joy is greater. Joy in this life is gaining good things, because the world is on your side. These two couplets stress that both rewards come together.

padaccheda.m: பிறர்கூறும் இன்சொல் தனக்கின்பம் பயத்தலை அனுபவித்து அறிகின்றவன்
அது நிற்கப் பிறர்மாட்டு வன்சொல்லைச் சொல்லுவது என்ன பயன் கருதி?

en.1: If you have seen what joy sweet words bring, why use hard words?
en.2: Someone who has felt the joy that others’ sweet words give him: what does he hope to gain by speaking hard words to others? Hard words are unpleasant to others too, so they shouldn’t be said.

padaccheda.m: அறம் பயக்கும் இனிய சொற்களும் தனக்கு உளவாயிருக்க அவற்றைக் கூறாது பாவம் பயக்கும் இன்னாத சொற்களை ஒருவன் கூறல்
இனிய கனிகளும் தன் கைக்கண் உளவாயிருக்க அவற்றை நுகராது இன்னாத காய்களை நுகர்ந்ததனோடு ஒக்கும்

en.1: To speak harsh words when sweet ones are there is like picking unripe fruit when ripe fruit is there.
en.2: To say harsh words that bring sin, when you have sweet words that bring righteousness, is like eating bitter unripe fruit when sweet ripe fruit is in your hand. The ripe fruit is like ambrosia and the unripe like poison. Harsh words end by hurting the one who says them. These two couplets tell the fault of harsh words.

padaccheda.m: தனக்கு முன்னோர் உதவி செய்யாதிருக்க ஒருவன் பிறனுக்குச் செய்த உதவிக்கு
மண்ணுலகும் விண்ணுலகுங் கைமாறாகக் கொடுத்தாலும் ஒத்தல்அரிது

en.1: For help you did nothing to earn, even earth and sky are hardly a fair return.
en.2: For help a person gives when you had done them no good first, even earth and heaven given in return can hardly match it. Every return has a cause, so none can match help with no cause. Some read a variant that makes this help given where it can’t be repaid.

padaccheda.m: ஒருவனுக்கு இறுதிவந்த எல்லைக்கண் ஒருவன் செய்த உபகாரம்
தன்னை நோக்கச் சிறிதாயிருந்ததாயினும் அக்காலத்தை நோக்க நிலவுலகத்தினும் மிகப் பெரிது

en.1: A good deed done at the right time, though small, is far greater than the world.
en.2: Help given when someone’s end has come may be small in itself, but judged by that moment it is far greater than the earth. You should look at the moment, not at the thing given.

padaccheda.w: பயன் தூக்கார் செய்த உதவி நயன் தூக்கின்
padaccheda.m: இவர்க்கு இதுசெய்தால் இன்னது பயக்கும் என்று ஆராய்தல் இலராய்ச் செய்த உதவியாகிய ஈரமுடைமையை ஆராயின்
அதன் நன்மை கடலினும் பெரிதாம்

en.1: Weigh the goodness of help given with no thought of return, and it is greater than the sea.
en.2: If you weigh the kindness in help given by those who never ask what it will bring, its goodness is greater than the sea. These three couplets say that help given without cause, at the right time, or without thought of return is boundless.

padaccheda.m: தமக்குத்தினை அளவிற்றாய உபகாரத்தை ஒருவன் செய்தானாயினும்
