en.2: Knowing that my lover inside would be hidden if my eyes blinked, I don’t blink. For that much, the town says he has given me the sickness of no sleep and has no loving-kindness. She is hurt that her friend doesn’t understand, so she says “this town” to set her apart. Don’t blame one who has never left.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, taking his side against her friend.

padaccheda.m: காதலர் எஞ்ஞான்றும் என் உள்ளத்துள்ளே உவந்து உறையா நிற்பர்
அதனை அறியாது அவரைப் பிரிந்து உறையா நின்றார், அன்பிலர் என்று சொல்லாநிற்கும் இவ்வூர்

en.1: He lives happily in my heart, always. This town says he lives apart from me, a stranger.
en.2: My lover always lives gladly in my heart. Not knowing this, the town says he lives away from me and has no loving-kindness. By “gladly” she shows that he has it. Don’t blame one who has neither left nor lost his loving-kindness.

uvacha.tr: Turned away by her friend and unable to bear it, he says this to her.

padaccheda.m: அரியராய மகளிரோடு காமத்தை அனுபவித்துப் பின் அதுபெறாது துன்புற்ற ஆடவர்க்கு
பண்டும் ஏமமாய் வருகின்ற மடல் அல்லது இனி எனக்கு வலியாவது இல்லை

en.1: For those who suffer and ache with desire, there is no refuge and no strength but the palmyra stalk.
en.2: Men who have enjoyed desire with women hard to reach, and then lost it, suffer. The palmyra stalk, their old protection, is now my only strength, because it brings that joy back and ends the pain. Men have long won joy this way. I counted on you to help me, in vain. Now that I know you won’t, I will win it this way too.

reading.note: The palmyra stalk, மடல், is the mock horse a spurned lover rides in public to press his claim on a woman.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: அவ்வருத்தத்தினைப் பொறாத உடம்பும் உயிரும் அதற்கு ஏமமாய மடன்மாவினை ஊரக் கருதாநின்றன
அதனை விலக்குவதாய நாணினை அகற்றி

en.1: My body and soul, which can’t bear this, will ride the palmyra stalk, putting shame aside.
en.2: My body and soul can’t bear this pain and mean to ride the palmyra horse that protects against it, having put aside the shame that would forbid it. Wisdom, self-control and the rest went first. Shame stayed, and now it has gone too. He says they will ride so that she sees how much he suffers and quickly grants what he asks.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நாணும் மிக்க ஆண்தகைமையும் யான் பண்டு உடையேன்
அவை காமத்தான் நீங்குதலான், அக்காமம் மிக்கார் ஏறும் மடலினை இன்று உடையேன்

en.1: Once I had shame and good manly strength. Today I have the palmyra stalk that people in desire ride.
en.2: Once I had shame and great manliness. Desire has driven them out, and today I have the palmyra stalk ridden by those overcome by desire. Shame stops you doing anything low, and manliness is standing firm before anything. Those were then. This is all I have now, so it will soon be done.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: யான் தன்னைக் கடத்தற்குக் கொண்ட நாணும் நல்லாண்மையும் ஆகிய புணைகளை
என்னிற் பிரித்துக் காமமாகிய கடியபுனல் கொண்டுபோகாநின்றது

en.1: The fierce flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and good manly strength.
en.2: I took shame and manliness as rafts to cross it. The fierce flood of desire tears them from me and carries them off. Other floods can’t do that, which is why he calls this one fierce. They are no rafts for this flood, and so they go.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: மாலைப் பொழுதின்கண் அனுபவிக்கும் துயரினையும், அதற்கு மருந்தாய மடலினையும் முன்னறியேன்
இதுபொழுது, எனக்கு மாலைபோலத் தொடர்ந்த சிறுவளையினை உடையாள் தந்தாள்

en.1: She of the small bangles strung like a garland gave me the palmyra stalk, and the sorrow that comes with the evening.
en.2: I never knew the sorrow of evening, or the stalk that is its medicine. She of the small bangles strung like a garland gave me both. Desire is there at other hours but flowers at evening, and the stalk comes from that, so she gave that disgrace too. She is so young she will say what you tell her. She gave these, so you can remove them.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நின்பேதை காரணமாக என்கண்கள் ஒருகாலும் துயிறலைப் பொருந்தா
அதனால் எல்லாரும் துயிலும் இடையாமத்தும் யான் இருந்து மடலூர்தலையே கருதாநிற்பன்

en.1: Even at midnight I think of riding the palmyra stalk. Because of this innocent girl my eyes won’t close.
en.2: Because of your innocent girl my eyes never close in sleep. So even at midnight, when everyone sleeps, I sit up thinking only of riding the stalk. “Innocent” speaks of her simplicity, not her age. Don’t put off what I ask until tomorrow.

uvacha.tr: He has blamed his sleeplessness on an innocent girl. Her friend says men have the wisdom women lack, so men should bear it. He answers.

padaccheda.w: கடல் அன்ன காமம் உழந்தும் மடல் ஏறாப் பெண்ணின்
padaccheda.m: கடல்போலக் கரையற்ற காமநோயினை அனுபவித்தும், மடல் ஊர்தலை்ச்செய்யாது ஆற்றியிருக்கும் பெண்பிறப்புபோல
மிக்க தகுதியினை உடைய பிறப்பு உலகத்தில் இல்லை

en.1: Nothing is greater than a woman, who suffers desire as vast as the sea and still doesn’t ride the palmyra stalk.
en.2: No birth in the world is as noble as a woman’s. She suffers the sickness of desire, shoreless as the sea, and bears it without riding the stalk. I wasn’t born to that, and you don’t see it. The man’s words end here, and from now on she speaks.

uvacha.tr: She is guarded more closely and her desire has grown. She says this to her friend.

padaccheda.m: இவர் நிறையால் நாம் மீதூர்தற்கு அரியர் என்று அஞ்சுதல் செய்யாது
மிகவும் அளிக்கத்தக்கார் என்று இரங்குதல் செய்யாது
மகளிர் காமமும் அவர் மறைத்தலைக் கடந்து மன்றின்கண்ணே வெளிப்படுவதாயிருந்தது

en.1: Desire doesn’t say, “They are too firm to overcome,” or “They deserve pity.” It breaks out of hiding into the open.
en.2: Desire doesn’t fear that women are too firm to be overcome, or pity them as deserving mercy. Even a woman’s desire gets past her hiding and shows in the open, before her father and brothers. Seeming to speak of women in general, she hints that her own desire has grown and that her love must now be made known.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: யான் முன் அடங்கி நிற்றலான் எல்லாரும் என்னை அறிதல் இலர், இனி அவ்வாறு நில்லாது யானே வெளி்ப்பட அறிவிப்பல் என்று கருதி
என்காமம் இவ்வூர் மறுகின்கண்ணே மயங்கிச் சுழலாநின்றது

en.1: Thinking that no one knows, my desire wanders the streets in a daze.
en.2: “I kept quiet before, so no one knows me. Now I will show myself.” With that thought my desire reels through the streets of this town. The daze means whispers, and the wandering means open gossip, and both have come. Now my love must be made known to my family.

uvacha.tr: Her friend has told her foster mother of the love, but jokes that she can’t think how to. Hurt, she says this to herself.

padaccheda.m: யாம் கேட்குமாறும் அன்றிக் கண்ணாற்காணுமாறு எம்மை அறிவிலார் நகாநின்றார்
அவர் அங்ஙனம் செய்கின்றது யாம் உற்றநோய்கள் தாம் உறாமையான்

en.1: Fools laugh in front of my eyes, because they haven’t suffered what I have.
en.2: Fools laugh at me, and not just where I can hear it but before my eyes, as they never did before. They do this because they haven’t suffered what I have. She doesn’t know her friend has told of her love, and is hurt that marriage isn’t coming, so she speaks of her as a stranger.

uvacha.tr: A false signal kept them apart. When he comes the next day, her friend tells him of the gossip and urges marriage. He answers.

padaccheda.m: மடந்தையொடு எம்மிடை நட்பு ஊரின்கண் அலராய் எழுதலான் அவளைப் பெறாது வருந்தும் என் அரிய உயிர் பெற்றது போன்று நிலைபெறும்
அந்நிலைபேற்றைத் தெய்வத்தால் யானே அறிவதல்லது கூறுகின்ற பலரும் அறியார்

en.1: The gossip keeps my precious life going. By good fortune, most people don’t know that.
en.2: As gossip about her and me rises in the town, my precious life, suffering without her, holds on as if I had her. By a god’s doing, only I know this and the many who talk don’t. The gossip makes a woman so hard to reach seem easy, so it props up his life. If they knew, they would stop, and his life would go.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: மலர்போலும் கண்ணையுடையாளது எய்தற்கு அருமை அறியாது
இவ்வூர் அவளை எளியளாக்கி அவளோடு அலர்கூறலை எமக்கு உபகரித்தது

en.1: Not knowing how rare she is, this woman with eyes like flowers, this town has made me a gift of gossip.
en.2: The town, not knowing how hard it is to reach this woman with eyes like flowers, makes her seem easy and kindly gives me gossip that links us. False signals and obstacles are what make her hard to reach. He says “gave” because the gossip is his support, and “this town” in thanks for the help.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: எங்கட்குக் கூட்டம் உண்மை இவ்வூர் அறிதலான் விளைந்த அலர் எனக்கு உறுவது ஒன்று அன்றோ
அது கேட்ட என் மனம், அக்கூட்டத்தைப் பெறாது இருந்தே பெற்றாற் போலும் நீர்மை உடைத்தாகலான்

en.1: Isn’t the gossip the town knows a good thing for me? It feels as if I have what I haven’t got.
en.2: The gossip that comes from the town knowing of our union: isn’t it just what suits me? Hearing it, my heart feels the joy of that union without having it.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: என் காமம் இவ்வூர் எடுக்கின்ற அலரானே அலர்தலை உடைத்தாயிற்று

padaccheda.w: அது இன்றேல் தன்மை இழந்து தவ் என்னும்
padaccheda.m: அவ்வலர் இல்லையாயின் தன் இயல்பு இழந்து சுருங்கும்

en.1: Gossip is what makes my desire grow. Without it, desire would lose its nature and shrink away.
en.2: My desire flowers on the gossip the town raises, and grows more and more. Without that gossip it would lose its nature, which is to give joy, and shrink to nothing.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: கள்உண்பார்க்குக் களிக்குந்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் இனிதாமாறுபோல
எனக்குக் காமம் அலராந்தோறும் இனிதாகாநின்றது

en.1: As getting drunk makes you want more toddy, so desire is sweeter each time it comes out in the open.
en.2: As drinking grows sweeter to drinkers each time they get drunk, my desire grows sweeter each time it becomes gossip. Such is the strength of my longing that even gossip gives me joy.

uvacha.tr: Obstacles and false signals keep her from him. With him within earshot, she speaks to her friend of the gossip, to press for marriage.

padaccheda.m: யான் காதலரைக் கண்ணுறப்பெற்றது ஒரு ஞான்றே
அதனின் ஆய அலர் அவ்வளவிற்றன்றித் திங்களைப் பாம்பு கொண்ட அலர்போன்று உலகெங்கும் பரந்தது

en.1: We saw each other just one day, yet the gossip is like the snake seizing the moon.
en.2: I saw my lover only once. The gossip from that hasn’t stopped there. It has spread through the whole world, like word of the snake seizing the moon. A love that spreads gossip even without meetings can’t go on. He must marry me.

uvacha.tr: Marriage is delayed and she can’t bear it. He is within earshot, and her friend tells her to bear up because of the gossip and her mother’s words. She answers.

padaccheda.m: இக்காம நோயாகிய பயிர்

padaccheda.w: ஊரவர் கௌவை எருவாக அன்னைசொல் நீராக நீளும்
padaccheda.m: இவ்வூரின் மகளிர் எடுக்கின்ற அலர் எருவாக அதுகேட்டு அன்னை வெகுண்டு சொல்லுகின்ற வெஞ்சொல் நீராக, வளராநின்றது

en.1: The town’s gossip is the manure and my mother’s words the water, and this sickness grows on.
en.2: This sickness of desire is a crop. The gossip raised by the women of the town is its manure, and the harsh words my mother says on hearing it are its water, and it grows. The very things that should shrink it make it spread. The aim is to make him marry her.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: ஏதிலார் எடுக்கின்ற அலரால் நாம் காமத்தை அவித்தும் என்று கருதுதல்
நெய்யால் எரியை அவித்தும் என்று கருதுதலோடு ஒக்கும்

en.1: To say you will put out desire with gossip is like saying you will put out a fire with ghee.
en.2: To think that the gossip strangers raise will put out our desire is like thinking that ghee will put out a fire. What stirs it up can’t put it out.

uvacha.tr: He has left, promising marriage, and she can’t bear it. He is back within earshot, and she answers her friend, who says to bear up for fear of gossip.

padaccheda.m: தம்மை எதிர்ப்பட்டஞான்று நின்னிற்பிரியேன் அஞ்சல் ஓ்ம்பு என்றவர்தாமே இன்று கண்டார் பலரும் நாணும் வகை நம்மைத் துறந்தபின்
நாம் ஏதிலார் கூறும் அலருக்கு நாணக்கூடுமோ, கூடாது

en.1: He told me not to be afraid, and then left me, to the shame of many. Can I still be ashamed of gossip?
en.2: The man who said when we met, “I won’t leave you, don’t be afraid,” has himself left me, so that all who see it are ashamed. Can I then feel shame at strangers’ gossip? I can’t. I am in a state that shames those who see me, so where would my shame come from?

uvacha.tr: With him within earshot, her friend speaks to her of the gossip, so that he will want to take her away with him.

padaccheda.m: உடன்போகற்கு ஏதுவாகல் நோக்கி யாம் பண்டே விரும்புவதாய அலரை இவ்வூர் தானே எடாநின்றது
இனிக் காதலர்தாமும் யாம் வேண்டியக்கால் அதனை இனிதின் நேர்வர், அதனால் இவ்வலர் நமக்கு நன்றாய் வந்தது

en.1: This town is raising the gossip we wanted. If he wishes, your lover will be kind.
en.2: We have long wanted this gossip, because it could lead to going away together, and the town is raising it for us. Now, if we ask, your lover will gladly agree, so the gossip has come as a good thing. She says “lover” to show that he loves us and won’t refuse.

reading.note: The words say “if he wishes”. He reads it as “if we ask”.

uvacha.tr: He says he will leave and come back soon. Her friend answers.

padaccheda.m: நீ எம்மைப் பிரியாமை உண்டாயின் அதனை எனக்குச்சொல்
அஃதுஒழியப் பிரிந்துபோய் விரைந்து வருதல் சொல்வையாயின், அதனை அப்பொழுது உயிர்வாழ்வார்க்குச் சொல்

en.1: If you aren’t going, tell me. If it is your quick return, tell that to whoever will still be alive.
en.2: If you won’t leave us, tell me that. If you mean to go and hurry back, tell that to those who will be alive then. She says “me”, not “her”, because she and her lady are one. Her lady can’t last until he returns and will die the moment he leaves. The aim is to stop him. Some take these as the woman’s own words.

uvacha.tr: She sees from his manner that he means to leave, and says this to her friend.

padaccheda.m: தழையும் கண்ணியும் கொண்டு பின்னின்ற ஞான்று அவர் நோக்குமாத்திரமும் புணர்ச்சி குறித்தமையான் நமக்கு இன்பம் உடைத்தாயிருக்கும்
இன்று அப்புணர்ச்சிதான் நிகழாநிற்கவும், அது பிரிவர் என்று அஞ்சும் அச்சத்தினை உடைத்தாயிற்று. அவர் அன்பின் நிலைமையிது

en.1: Even a look from him used to be sweet. Now our union itself holds the pain of fearing he will leave.
en.2: When he stood waiting with his gifts of leaves and garlands, even his look was sweet to us, because it promised union. Now union itself carries the fear that he will leave. That is what his love has come to. His special tenderness shows he means to go, and that frightens her. The aim is to stop him.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: பிரியேன் என்ற தம்சொல்லும் நம்பிரிவாற்றாமையும் அறிதல் உடையராய கண்ணும்
ஒரோவழிப் பிரிவு நிகழ்தலான்
அவர்சொல்லும் தலையளியும்பற்றி நம்மாட்டு அன்புடையர் எனத் தேறும் தேற்றம் அரிதாயிருந்தது

en.1: It is hard to trust. Even those who understand can sometimes leave.
en.2: Even one who remembers his own word, “I won’t leave,” and knows I can’t bear parting may sometimes leave. So it is hard to feel sure, from his words and his tenderness, that he loves me.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: எதிர்ப்பட்ட ஞான்றே தலையளி செய்து, 'நின்னிற்பிரியேன் அஞ்சல்' என்றவர்தாமே பின் பிரிவாராயின்
அவர்க்குஅன்றி அவர் தெளிவித்த சொல்லை மெய்யெனத் தெளிந்தார்க்குக் குற்றமுண்டோ?

en.1: If the one who was tender and said “Don’t be afraid” goes away, is there any fault in those who trusted what he swore?
en.2: He was tender when we met and said, “I won’t leave you, don’t be afraid.” If he now leaves, is the fault in those who believed his assuring words? She speaks of herself as someone else. The fault of word and deed not matching will be his, so stop him and spare him that.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: என்னுயிரைச் செல்லாமற் காத்தியாயின், அதனை ஆளுதற்கு அமைந்தாருடைய செலவினை அழுங்குவிப்பாயாக
அழுங்குவிப்பார் இன்றி, அவர்செல்வாராயின் அவரால் ஆளப்பட்ட உயிரும் செல்லும், சென்றால் பின் அவரைக்கூடுதல் எனக்கு அரிதாம்

en.1: If you would save me, stop the one who is mine from leaving. If he goes, it will be hard to meet again.
en.2: If you would keep my life from going, stop the leaving of the one fit to rule it. If no one stops him and he goes, the life he rules goes too, and then I can’t join him again. Fit to rule means made her lord by a god’s will.

uvacha.tr: Her friend comes and tells her that he has said he is leaving. She answers.

padaccheda.m: நம் கவவுக்கடுமை அறிந்த தலைவர்தாமே நம்முனின்று தம்பிரிவினை உணர்த்தும் வன்கண்மை உடையராயின்
அத்தன்மையார் பின்பு நம் ஆற்றாமை அறிந்து வந்து தலையளிசெய்வார் என்று இருக்கும் ஆசை விடப்படும்

en.1: If he is hard enough to tell me he’s leaving, there is little hope that he will be kind.
en.2: He knows how tightly I hold him. If he is hard enough to stand before me and speak of leaving, give up hope that he will see my pain, come back and be tender. If he could plan and announce it while we were together, without loving-kindness, how would he remember me with it once gone? The aim is to stop him.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: துறைவன் என்னைப் பிரியலுற்றமையை
அவன் உணர்த்தாமல் தாமே உணர்ந்து என் முன்கையிறையினின்றும் கழலாநின்ற வளைகள் என்க்கு அறிவியாவோ, அவன் உணர்த்த உணர்ந்துவந்து நீ அறிவித்தல் வேண்டுமோ

en.1: Won’t these bangles slipping from my forearm spread the word that the lord of the shore has left me?
en.2: These bangles slipping from my wrist knew it without being told. Won’t they tell me that the lord of the shore means to leave? Did you have to come and say it? She speaks as if it has happened, and on hearing it she has grown thin. You should have stopped him, not brought word. You have only done what the bangles did. She says this in hurt.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: மகளிர்க்குத் தம் குறிப்பறியும் தோழியர் இல்லாத வேற்றூரின்கண் வாழ்தல் இன்னாது
அதன்மேலும் தம் காதலரைப் பிரிதல் அதனினும் இன்னாது

en.1: It is painful to live in a town without your own people. More painful still is parting from those dear to you.
en.2: For women it is painful to live in a strange town with no friends who understand them. More painful still is parting from their lover. She is hurt that her friend agreed to his going instead of stopping him, so she speaks of a town without your own people. Seeming to speak in general, she means both are true of her.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says desire, like fire, burns only where it stands, so she must bear it. She answers.

padaccheda.m: தீத் தன்னைத் தொட்டாற் சுடுமாயின் சுடுதல்அல்லது
காமமாகிய நோய்போலத் தன்னை அகன்றாற் தப்பாது சுடுதலைவற்றோ, மாட்டாது

en.1: Fire burns if you touch it. Can it burn when you leave it, as the sickness of desire does?
en.2: Fire burns when touched, if it burns at all. Can it, like the sickness of desire, burn without fail when you go away from it? It can’t. “If it burns” allows that spells and medicines can stop a fire, and desire has no such cure. How am I to bear what is crueller than fire?

uvacha.tr: Her friend says many women bear parting, and she isn’t doing so. She answers.

padaccheda.w: (நீ சொல்லுகின்றது ஒக்கும்) அரிது ஆற்றி அல்லல் நோய் நீக்கி
padaccheda.m: பிரிவு உணர்த்தியவழி அதற்கு உடம்பட்டுப் பிரியுங்கால் நிகலும் அல்லல் நோயினையும் நீக்கி

padaccheda.w: பிரிவு ஆற்றிப் பின் இருந்து வாழ்வார் பலர்
padaccheda.m: பிரிந்தால் அப்பிரிவுதன்னையும் ஆற்றிப் பின்னும் இருந்து உயிர்வாழும் மகளிர் உலகத்துப் பலர்

en.1: Many do the hard thing, drive off the sickness of grief, bear the parting and go on living afterwards.
en.2: What you say is true. Many women agree to parting, which is hard, rid themselves of its grief, bear it and go on living. Yet the worry over where he is, the pangs of desire, the lute, the moon and the breeze are hard to bear. No woman who can’t live without her lover survives all that, and she too will die.

reading.note: The words say many survive parting. He hears bitter irony: no woman who truly needs her lover survives it, and she won’t either.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says that showing the sickness of desire doesn’t suit her sense of shame. She answers.

padaccheda.m: இந்நோயைப் பிறர் அறிதல் நாணி யான் மறையாநின்றேன்
நிற்பவும், இஃது அந்நாள்வரை நில்லாது நீர் வேண்டும் என்று இறைப்பவர்க்கு ஊற்றுநீர் மிகுமாறு போல் மிகாநின்றது

en.1: I would hide this sickness, but it rises like spring water for those who draw it.
en.2: Ashamed that others should know, I hide this sickness. But it won’t stay hidden. It rises as spring water rises for those who draw it because they need it. So what use is hiding? Now you must do what comes next.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says she must do one of two things: hide it from the people here, or send word to him. She answers.

padaccheda.m: இந்நோயை ஈண்டையார் அறியாமல் மறைத்தலும் வல்லேன் ஆகின்றிலேன்
ஆகாக்கால், நோய்செய்தார்க்கு உரைக்கவெனின், அதுவும் எனக்கு நாணினைத் தாராநின்றது, இனி என்செய்கோ?

en.1: I can’t hide this sickness, and telling the one who caused it brings me shame.
en.2: I can’t hide this sickness from the people here, because it grows hour by hour. Telling the one who caused it brings shame too, because a message to one gone far would say that I am still alive. What am I to do?

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: காமநோயும் அதனைச் செய்தவர்க்கு உரைக்கல் ஒல்லாத நாணும்
தம்மைப் பொறாத என் உடம்பின்கண்ணே
உயிர் காத் தண்டாக அதன் இருதலையினும் தூங்காநின்றன

en.1: Desire and shame hang from my life as from a carrying pole, inside this body that can’t bear them.
en.2: The sickness of desire, and the shame that won’t let me tell him, hang in my failing body from the two ends of my life, as from a carrying pole. They balance exactly. One urges her to send word and the other forbids it, and together they are breaking her life. She can’t settle on either, so it will snap.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says women like her don’t fall into the sea of desire, and if they do they cross it on a fitting raft. She answers.

padaccheda.m: யாவர்க்கும் உளவாய் வருகின்ற இவ்விரண்டன்உள்ளும், எனக்குண்டாகின்றது காமக்கடலே
அதனை நீந்தும் அரணாகிய புணை இல்லை

en.1: There is indeed a sea of desire. There is no safe raft to cross it.
en.2: Of the two things that everyone may have, what I have is the sea of desire. The safe raft to cross it, I don’t have. The point is that you should have been that raft by sending word, and you haven’t.

uvacha.tr: Hurt that no word has been sent to him, she says this to her friend.

padaccheda.m: இன்பம் செய்தற்குரிய நட்பின்கண்ணே துன்ப வரவினைச் செய்யவல்லவர்
துன்பம் செய்தற்கு உரிய பகைமைக்கண் என்செய்வர் கொலோ?

en.1: Those who can bring suffering even in friendship, what would they do in enmity?
en.2: Those able to bring suffering into friendship, which should give joy, what would they do in enmity, which is meant to give pain? We have never seen them as enemies, so we can’t know. She is hurt that her friend doesn’t stop the suffering, so she blames her for it and speaks of her as someone else.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says those who have had joy from desire will have pain from it too. She answers.

padaccheda.m: காமம் புணர்வால் இன்பம் செய்யுங்கால், அவ்வின்பம் கடல்போலப் பெரிதாம்

padaccheda.w: மற்று அஃது அடுங்கால் துன்பம் அதனின் பெரிது
padaccheda.m: இனி அதுதானே பிரிவால் துன்பம் செய்யுங்கால், அத்துன்பம் அக்கடலினும் பெரிதாம்

en.1: The joy of desire is a sea. But when it turns on you, the pain is greater than that sea.
en.2: When desire gives joy through union, that joy is as great as the sea. When the same desire gives pain through parting, the pain is greater than the sea. If it only matched the joy received it could be borne, but it doesn’t.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says the sea of desire can be crossed with self-control as the raft. She answers.

en.1: I swim the fierce flood of desire and see no shore. Even at midnight I alone am here.
en.2: I have swum the sea of desire, yet I find no shore. In the dead of night, when everyone sleeps, I am alone with no companion. And I don’t die and escape, but stay alive. What a fruit of evil deeds this is! “Alone” hints that you have been no companion to me.

uvacha.tr: She speaks of the cruelty of the night and grieves.

padaccheda.m: இவ்விரா அளித்தாய் இருந்தது

padaccheda.w: மன் உயிர் எல்லாம் துயிற்றி என்னல்லது துணை இல்லை
padaccheda.m: உலகத்து நிலைபெறுகின்ற உயிர்களையெல்லாம் தானே துயிலப்பண்ணுதலான் என்னை அல்லது வேறு துணை உடைத்தாயிற்றில்லை

en.1: Poor night. It has put all living things to sleep and has no companion but me.
en.2: This night is a poor thing. It has itself put all the world’s living things to sleep, and so has no companion but me. It lets go all who could keep it company and takes me, who am close to death. That is senseless, so she calls it pitiable, in scorn.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, grieving at the night.

padaccheda.m: காதலரொடு நாம் இன்புற்ற முன்னாள்களில் குறியவாய் அவர் பிரிவு ஆற்றேமாகின்ற இந்நாள்களிலே நெடியவாய்ச் செல்கின்ற கங்குல்கள்
அக்கொடியாரது கொடுமைக்கு மேலே தாம் கொடுமை செய்யாநின்றன

en.1: Crueller even than that cruel one’s cruelty are these nights that now drag on.
en.2: The nights were short in the days of joy with my lover. In these days, when I can’t bear his absence, they are long, and they add their cruelty to his. She calls him cruel because he left without a thought for her pain. His cruelty is delaying his return. The nights have no pity for what that does to her.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says she shouldn’t weep, because her eyes are losing their great beauty. She answers.

padaccheda.m: மனம்போலக் காதலர் உள்ள தேயத்துக் கடிதின் செல்லவல்லனவாயின்
என் கண்கள் இங்ஙனம் வெள்ளமாகிய தந்நீரை நீந்தா

en.1: If my eyes could go where he is, as my heart does, they wouldn’t be swimming in this flood of water.
en.2: If they could travel quickly to where my lover is, as my heart can, my eyes wouldn’t swim in this flood of their own water. They can’t, so swimming is all that is left to them. The heart travels by thought, but a body must walk, so the eyes can’t go with it and see him. This opens the next chapter.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says her weeping eyes are losing their beauty and she must bear up. She answers.

padaccheda.w: தண்டா நோய் யாம் கண்டது தாம் காட்ட
padaccheda.m: இத்தணியா நோயை யாம் அறிந்தது, தாம் எமக்குக் காதலரைக் காட்டலான் அன்றோ? கண்தாம் கழுல்வது எவன்கொல்= அன்று அத்தொழிலவாய கண்கள் இன்று எம்மைக் காட்டச்சொல்லி அழுகின்றது என்கருதி?

en.1: Why do my eyes weep now? It was through their showing that I came to see this endless sickness.
en.2: I came to know this unending sickness because my eyes showed me my lover. Why do those same eyes now weep, telling me to show him to them? Today too, only they can show him. How could I?

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: மேல்விளைவதனை ஆராய்ந்து அறியாது அன்று காதலரை நோக்கிநின்ற உண்கண்கள்
இன்று இது நம்மால் வந்ததுஆகலின் பொறுத்தல் வேண்டும் எனக் கூறுபடுத்து உணராது துன்பமுழப்பது என்கருதி?

en.1: These kohl-lined eyes looked without knowing what would come. Why do they now suffer, not understanding?
en.2: My kohl-lined eyes looked at my lover that day without weighing what would follow: that he would go and not come back. Why do they suffer now, instead of reasoning that this came through them and must be borne? If you don’t guard against a thing, bearing it is all that’s left. Not even doing that is utter folly.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.w: தாம் கதுமென நோக்கித் தாமே கழுலும் இது
padaccheda.m: இக்கண்கள் அன்று காதலரைத் தாமே விரைந்து நோக்கி இன்றும் தாமே இருந்து அழுகின்ற இது
நம்மால் சிரிக்கத்தக்க இயல்பினை உடைத்து

en.1: My eyes rushed to look, and now they weep by themselves. There is something laughable in this.
en.2: These eyes rushed to look at my lover that day of their own accord, and now they sit weeping of their own accord. This folly is something for me to laugh at. It brings laughter from those who guard against a thing before it comes.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: உண்கண்கள்

padaccheda.w: உயல் ஆ்ற்றா உய்வுஇல் நோய் என்கண் நிறுத்து
padaccheda.m: அன்று யான் உய்யமாட்டாமைக்கு ஏதுவாய ஒழிவில்லாத நோயை என்கண்ணே நிறுத்தி
தாமும் அழுதலைமாட்டாவண்ணம் நீர் வற்றிவிட்டன

en.1: My kohl-lined eyes have left in me a sickness I can’t escape or survive, and now they can’t weep, their water gone.
en.2: That day my kohl-lined eyes fixed in me an endless sickness that I can’t escape. Now their water has dried up and they can’t even weep. They fixed it there by showing me one who would leave and not return. They did me harm first, and harm has come to them.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: எனக்குக்கடலும் சிறிதாகும்வண்ணம் பெரிதாய காமநோயைச் செய்த என்கண்கள்
அத்தீவினையாற் தாமும் துயில்கிலவாய்த் துன்பத்தையும் உழவாநின்றன

en.1: My eyes, which gave me a sickness of desire too great for the sea, now suffer and can’t close.
en.2: My eyes gave me a sickness of desire so great that the sea seems small. For that evil deed they suffer too and can’t sleep. Desire came through seeing, so she blames the eyes for it. Their suffering is their weeping.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.w: எமக்கு இந்நோய் செய்த கண் தாஅம் இதற்படடது
padaccheda.m: எமக்கு இக்காமநோயினைச் செய்த கண்கள் தாமும், இத்துயிலாது அழுதற்கண்ணேபட்டது
மிகவும் இனிதாயிற்று

en.1: Oh, how sweet! The eyes that gave me this sickness have fallen into it themselves.
en.2: The eyes that gave me this sickness of desire have themselves fallen into this sleepless weeping. How very sweet! To me, whom they made suffer, it is as if the pain had ended.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: விழைந்து உண்ணெகிழ்ந்து, விடாதே அன்று அவரைக் கண்ட கண்கள்
இன்று இத்துயிலாது அழுங்கலாய துன்பத்தினை, உழந்து உழந்து தம் அகத்துள்ள நீர் அற்றே போக!

en.1: Let them suffer and suffer till their water runs out, these eyes that longed and longed and begged to see him.
en.2: Those eyes longed and melted that day and wouldn’t let him out of their sight. Let them suffer this sleepless weeping on and on, until the water inside them is gone!

uvacha.tr: Her friend says he hasn’t really gone, he is here, and she must bear up until she sees him. She answers.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சத்தால் விழையாது வைத்துச் சொன்மாத்திரத்தால் விழைந்தவர் இவ்விடத்தே உளர்
அவ்வுண்மையாற் பயன் யாது? அவரைக் கண்கள் காணாது அமைகின்றன இல்லையாயின

en.1: There is one who wanted me without cherishing me. Still, my eyes will not rest until they see him.
en.2: The one who wanted me in words but not in his heart is right here. What use is that? My eyes won’t rest without seeing him. His actions showed no care, though he spoke of fearing to part and of coming back. I can bear it, but my eyes can’t. With another reading: are there any in the world who want one who doesn’t want them?

uvacha.tr: Her friend says she must bear up and let her eyes sleep. She answers.

padaccheda.m: காதலர் வாராத ஞான்று அவர் வரவுபார்த்துத் துயிலா
வந்த ஞான்று அவர் பிரிவஞ்சித் துயிலா
ஆதலால் அவ்விரு வழியும் என் கண்கள் பொறுத்தற்கு அரிய துன்பத்தினை உடைய

en.1: When he doesn’t come they don’t sleep. When he comes they don’t sleep. Either way my eyes are in deep pain.
en.2: When my lover hasn’t come, my eyes stay awake watching for him. When he has come, they stay awake fearing he will leave. Both ways they suffer past bearing. They will never have sleep.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says she must hide his cruelty, so that the town won’t speak ill of him. She answers.

padaccheda.w: எம்போல் அறைபறை கண்ணார் அகத்து மறை பெறல்
padaccheda.m: எம்மைப்போலும் அறைபறையாகிய கண்ணினை உடையார் தம் நெஞ்சின்கண் அடக்கிய மறையை அறிதல்
இவ்வூரின்கண் உள்ளார்க்கு எளிது

en.1: It isn’t hard for the town to find out the secret of those like me, whose eyes are beaten drums.
en.2: The town finds it easy to learn the secret held in the hearts of those like me, whose eyes are drums being beaten. Eyes and drums alike tell the world outside what is inside. Though I hide it, these eyes make it known.

uvacha.tr: She agreed to the parting earlier. Now she can’t bear it and has turned pale, and she says this to herself.

padaccheda.m: என்னை நயந்தவர்க்கு அதுபொழுது பிரிவை உடம்பட்ட நான்
அதனை ஆற்றாது இதுபொழுது பசந்த என் இயல்பினை யார்க்குச் சொல்வேன்

en.1: I agreed to go without the kindness of the one who loved me. Who can I tell now that I have turned pale?
en.2: I agreed to the parting for the one who loves me. Now I can’t bear it and have turned pale. Whom can I tell? She calls him loving because he told her first, ready to stay if she refused. Her consent means he will leave again, so union will be hard. She brought this on herself, so telling anyone would be a reproach.

uvacha.tr: Her friend worries that she can’t bear it. She answers, to say that she can.

padaccheda.m: இப்பசப்புத்தான்
என்னைஉண்டாக்கினார் அவர் என்னும் பெருமிதத்தான்
என்மேனியை மேற்கொண்டு செலுத்தாநின்றது

en.1: Proud to say “He gave me,” pallor climbs on my body and rides it.
en.2: I am bearing up, but this pallor, proud that he gave birth to it, has mounted my body and drives it on. It rides by right, so you needn’t worry.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says she must bear up, so that her beauty and her shame aren’t lost. She answers.

padaccheda.m: பிரிகின்ற ஞான்றே அவ்விரண்டற்கும் தலைமாறாக இக்காமநோயினையும் பசலையையும் எனக்குத் தந்து
என் மேனியழகினையும், நாணினையும் அவர் கொண்டுபோயினார்

en.1: He took my beauty and my shame, and in exchange gave me sickness and pallor.
en.2: When he left he gave me this sickness of desire and this pallor, and in exchange took away my beauty and my shame. Sickness takes the place of shame because it grows the more she holds it down. Unless he gives them back, those won’t return and these won’t go.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says she knows his reassuring words and his goodness, so he won’t be long. She answers.

padaccheda.m: அவர் சொற்களை யான் மனத்தால் நினையாநிற்பேன்
வாக்கால் உரைப்பதும், அவர் நற்றிறங்களையே
அங்ஙனம் செய்யாநிற்கவும், பசப்பு வந்துநின்றது, இது வஞ்சனையாய் இருந்தது

en.1: I think of him, and what I talk of is his worth. So is this pallor a fraud?
en.2: I keep his words in my mind, and all I speak of is his goodness. Yet pallor has come, and this is treachery. The body follows mind and speech, so it shouldn’t have come there either. She says this to show that she is bearing up.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says he has gone only a little way, and still she can’t bear it. She tells what happened before.

padaccheda.m: பண்டும் காதலர் உங்கே செல்வாராக
என்மேனி பசப்பூர்வது இங்கேயன்றோ, அப்பெற்றியது இன்று பிறிதொன்றாமோ

en.1: Look there, my lover going away. Look here, pallor spreading over my body.
en.2: Before too, as my lover was going over there, my body was turning pale over here. Is it any different today? His going and the coming of pallor are like day going and night coming. You know this, so why do you speak as if you don’t?

uvacha.tr: She goes on, telling her friend what happened before.

padaccheda.m: விளக்கினது மெலிவுபார்த்து நெருங்கிவரும் இருளேபோல
கொண்கன் முயக்கினது மெலிவுபார்த்து நெருங்கிவரும் இப்பசப்பு

en.1: As darkness waits for a lamp to fail, pallor waits for my husband’s embrace to slacken.
en.2: As darkness watches for a lamp to weaken and closes in, this pallor watches for my husband’s embrace to weaken and closes in. If it looks for its chance even while he stays, what won’t it do once he has left?

uvacha.tr: She goes on, telling her friend what happened before.

padaccheda.m: முன்ஒருஞான்று காதலரைப் புல்லிக்கிடந்த யான் அறியாது புடைபெயர்ந்தேன்
அப்புடைபெயர்ந்த அளவிலே பசப்பு அள்ளிக்கொள்வதுபோல வந்து செறிந்தது

en.1: I lay holding him and shifted a little. That was enough: pallor came on so thick you could scoop it up.
en.2: Once, lying in my lover’s arms, I moved aside without knowing it. At just that, pallor closed in so thick it could be scooped up. If a mere shift did that, need I say what this parting does?

uvacha.tr: Her friend says she shouldn’t turn pale like this. Hurt, she answers.

padaccheda.m: இவள் ஆற்றியிராது பசந்தாள் என்று என்னைப் பழிகூறுவதல்லது
இவளை அவர் துறந்து போயினார் என்று அவரைக் கூறுவார் ஒருவரும் இல்லை

en.1: People say, “She has turned pale.” No one says, “He has left her.”
en.2: They blame me, saying she couldn’t bear up and has turned pale. No one says that he has left her and gone. She says “they” to set her friend apart, hurt that her friend presses only her.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, hurt, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: இப்பிரிவை யானே உடம்படும்வகை சொல்லியவர் இன்று நின் கருத்தான் நல்லநிலையினர் ஆவராயின்
என்மேனி பட்டதுபடப் பசப்பதாக

en.1: Let my body turn as pale as it will, if the one who talked me into this is then in the right.
en.2: In your view the man who talked me into this parting stands on good ground. Then let my body turn pale as it may. I didn’t know how cruel this parting would be, and he talked me into it and left. He must be found blameless, so what does it matter what happens to my body and its pallor?

uvacha.tr: To help her bear the parting her friend speaks ill of him, and she takes his side.

padaccheda.m: அன்று, தாம் குறைநயப்பித்துக் கூடினவர்க்கு இன்று நல்காமையை நட்டார் தூற்றார் ஆயின்
பசப்புற்றாள் என வேற்றுமையான் அன்றிப் பசப்புத்தான் ஆயினாள், என ஒற்றுமையால் தாம் சொல்ல அ்பபெயரைப் பெறுதல் எனக்கு நன்று

en.1: It is well to be called pallor itself, if people don’t spread it about that the one who won me is unkind.
en.2: He pressed his suit and won me, and now isn’t kind. If his friends don’t spread word of that, it is well for me to be named Pallor, as if I were pallor itself. She can’t stand his being blamed and says this in scorn. Let them not say he has no compassion. Let them go on saying she has turned pale. That is how she can bear it.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says he can bear this even less than she can, so he will soon come, and she will have great joy with him. She answers.

padaccheda.m: தம்மாற் காதலிக்கப்படும் கணவர் தம்மைக் காதலிக்கப்பெற்ற மகளிர்
பெற்றார் அன்றே, காமநுகர்ச்சி என்னும் பரல் இல்லாத கனியை

en.1: Those whose love is returned by the one they love have found the stoneless fruit of desire.
en.2: Women loved by the husbands they love have surely received the stoneless fruit, the enjoyment of desire. They have received it, because it can’t be had without good deeds done before. It is stoneless, because nothing hinders it. Our lover has left and won’t return, so we haven’t received that fruit.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: அறமும் பொருளும் நோக்கிப் பிரிந்தால் தம்மை இன்றியமையா மகளிர்க்கு அவரை இன்றியமையாக் கணவர் அளவறிந்து வந்துசெய்யும் தலையளி
தன்னையே நோக்கி உயிர்வாழ்வார்க்கு வானம் அளவறிந்து பெய்தாற்போலும்

en.1: The kindness of lovers to those who love them is like rain from the sky to those who live by it.
en.2: When men leave for righteousness and wealth, husbands who can’t do without their wives come back in due measure and show them tenderness. This is like the sky raining in due measure on those who live by it. Our lover doesn’t want us, so we have no such tenderness. Like those who live by rain in a drought, we can only die.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: தாம் விழையும் கணவரான் விழையப்படும் மகளிர்க்கு ஏற்புடைத்து
காதலர் பிரிந்தாராயினும் நம்மை நினைந்து கடிதின் வருவர், வந்தால் நாம் இன்புற்று வாழ்தும் என்றிருக்கும் தருக்கு

en.1: Only those loved by the ones they love can have the pride of saying, “We will live.”
en.2: Women wanted by the husbands they want may well have this proud thought: though he has left, he will think of us and soon come, and then we will live in joy. He doesn’t want us, so what suits us is death.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says that by hiding his lack of compassion she shows a god-like chastity and will be honoured by chaste women. She answers.

padaccheda.m: கற்புடைமகளிரால் நன்கு மதிக்கப்படுவாரும்

padaccheda.w: தாம் வீழ்வார் வீழப்படார் எனின் கெழீஇ இலர்
padaccheda.m: தாம் விரும்பும் கணவரான் விரும்பப்படாராயின் தீவினையாட்டியர்

en.1: Even those who are held dear are without blessing, if the one they love doesn’t love them back.
en.2: Even women honoured by chaste women are sinners, if the husbands they love don’t love them. Having no good deeds means having evil ones. Such honour is no use to me, with my evil deeds.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says that because she loves him she has understood his purpose and borne up. She answers.

padaccheda.m: நம்மாற் காதல் செய்யப்பட்டவர் நமக்கு என்ன இன்பத்தைச் செய்வர்
அவ்வாறே தாமும் நங்கண் காதல் செய்யாவழி

en.1: What can the one I love do for me, if he doesn’t love me too?
en.2: What joy can the one we love give us, if he doesn’t love us as we love him? All our love has brought us is pain.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: மகளிர் ஆடவர் என்னும் இருதலையினும் வேட்கை ஒருதலைக்கண்ணேயாயின் அஃது இன்னாது
காவினது பாரம்போல இருதலைக்கண்ணும் ஒப்பின், அஃது இனிது

en.1: Desire on one side only is painful. Like the load on a carrying pole, it is sweet when it is on both sides.
en.2: When longing is on one side only, the woman’s or the man’s, it is painful. When it is equal on both sides, like the loads on a carrying pole, it is sweet. If the longing in me were in him too, would I suffer like this?

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: காமம் நுகர்தற்குரிய இருவரிடத்தும் ஒப்பநிற்றல் ஒழித்து, ஒருவரிடத்தே நின்று பொருகின்ற காமக்கடவுள்
அவ்விடத்துப் பசப்பானாய பருவரலும் படர்மிகுதியும் அறியான்கொல்லோ

en.1: The god of desire stays on one side only. Doesn’t he see my pain and my grief?
en.2: The god of desire should stand equally with both lovers, yet he stands with one and attacks her. Doesn’t he know the pain of her pallor and the flood of her grief? Even a god, who without liking or dislike should know all that happens in everyone, has turned against me. How can I escape now?

uvacha.tr: No messenger comes from him, and she says this.

padaccheda.m: தம்மால் விரும்பப்படும் காதலர் திறத்துநின்று ஓர் இன்சொல்லளவும் பெறாதே பிரிவாற்றி உயிர்வாழ்கின்ற மகளிர்போல
வன்கண்மையுடையார் இவ்வுலகத்து இல்லை

en.1: No one in the world is as hard as those who go on living without a sweet word from the one they love.
en.2: No one in the world is as hard as women who bear parting and stay alive without even one sweet word about the lover they want. She says “sweet word” because any word about him would be sweet to her. I am hard, for I live on without even that.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, with still no messenger from him.

padaccheda.m: என்னால் நச்சப்பட்ட காதலர் என்மாட்டு அன்பிலரே ஆயினும்
அவர் திறத்து யாதானும் ஓர் சொல்லும் என் செவிக்கு இனியவாம்

en.1: Even if the one I long for isn’t kind to me, any word of him is sweet to my ears.
en.2: Though the lover I long for has no loving-kindness towards me, any word about him is sweet to my ears. Even the word that he isn’t coming would do. I haven’t had even that.

uvacha.tr: No messenger comes from him. Thinking of sending one herself, she says this to her heart.

padaccheda.m: நின்னொடு உறாதார்க்கு நின்னுறுநோயை உரைக்கலுற்ற நெஞ்சே
நீ ஆற்றாய் ஆயினும் அரிதாய அதனையொழிந்து, நினக்குத் துயரம்செய்கின்ற கடலைத் தூர்க்க முயல்வாயாக, அஃது எளிது

en.1: Long may you live, my heart. You would tell your sickness to one who isn’t close to you. Fill in the sea instead.
en.2: Heart, you are about to tell your sickness to one who is nothing to you. If you can’t bear it, drop that hard task and try filling in the sea that torments you, which is easy. The sickness is past telling and the listener is no kin, so it can’t work, and would do no good if it did. So she says “long may you live” in mockery.

uvacha.tr: He says this to his companion, who has gone as a messenger.

padaccheda.m: முன் கூடியஞான்றை இன்பத்தினைப் பிரி்ந்துழி நினைந்தாலும், அதுபொழுது பெற்றாற்போல நீங்காத மகிழ்ச்சியைத் தருதலால்
உண்டுழியல்லது மகிழ்ச்சி செய்யாத கள்ளினும் காமம் இன்பம் பயத்தலுடைத்து

en.1: Desire is sweeter than toddy, because even thinking of it brings a great joy that doesn’t fade.
en.2: Thinking in absence of the joy of past union gives an unfading gladness, as if it were happening now. So desire gives more joy than toddy, which delights only when drunk. He is telling of his loneliness and that he hasn’t forgotten.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to his companion.

padaccheda.w: தாம் வீழ்வார் நினைப்ப வருவது ஒன்று இல்
padaccheda.m: தம்மால் விரும்பப்படுவாரைப் பிரிவின்கண் நினைத்தால் அந்நினைவார்க்கு அப்பிரிவான் வருவதோர் துன்பம் இல்லையாம்
அதனாற் காமம் எத்துணையும் இனிதுஒன்றேகாண்

en.1: Desire is sweet in every way. When you think of the one you love, no pain comes.
en.2: When you think in parting of the one you love, no pain of parting comes to you. So desire is sweet in every degree, as sweet apart as together. He is saying how he has borne it.

uvacha.tr: Thinking of him and suffering, she says this to her friend.

padaccheda.m: எனக்குத் தும்மல் எழுவது போன்று தோன்றிக் கெடாநின்றது
அதனாற் காதலர் என்னைநினைப்பார் போன்று நினையார் ஆகல்வேண்டும்

en.1: A sneeze starts to come and then dies away. Does he seem about to think of me, and then not?
en.2: A sneeze seems about to rise in me and dies away. So my lover must seem about to think of me, and then not. People say a sneeze comes when dear ones far away think of you. She says this on sensing that the work he went for, which seemed about to end, hasn’t ended.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: எம்முடைய நெஞ்சத்து அவர் எப்பொழுதும் உளரேயாய் இராநின்றார்
அவ்வகையே அவருடைய நெஞ்சத்தும் யாமும் உளம் ஆதுமோ, ஆகேமோ

en.1: Am I too in his heart? In mine, oh, he is always there.
en.2: He is always in my heart, without a break. Am I in his in the same way, or not? Is he staying away, though I am there, because his work isn’t done? Or is it done, and he stays away because I am not there?

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: தம்முடைய நெஞ்சின்கண்ணே யாம் செல்லாமல் எம்மைக் காவல்கொண்ட காதலர்
தாம் எம்முடைய நெஞ்சின்கண் ஒழியாது வருதலை நாணார் கொல்லோ

en.1: He has barred me from his heart. Isn’t he ashamed to keep coming into mine?
en.2: My lover has set a guard in his heart so that I can’t enter. Isn’t he ashamed to keep coming into mine without end? To never let someone come to you, yet go to them again and again, isn’t what a person with shame does.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says that remembering the joy of their union is killing her, and she should forget it. She answers.

padaccheda.m: யான் அவரோடு புணர்ந்தஞான்றை இன்பத்தை நினைதலான் இத்துன்ப வெள்ளத்தும் உயிர்வாழ்கின்றேன்
அது இன்றாயின், வேறு எத்தால் உயிர்வாழ்வேன்

en.1: How else would I live? I live by remembering the days I was with him.
en.2: I stay alive in this flood of pain by thinking of the joy of the days I joined him. Without that, what would I live by? Other things could sustain life, such as a messenger from him or one of my own, but I have none of them. This is my only support.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, answering her friend.

padaccheda.m: அவ்வின்பத்தை மறத்தல் அறியேனாய் இன்று உள்ளாநிற்கவும், பிரிவு என் உள்ளத்தைச் சுடாநின்றது
அங்ஙனம் பிரிவு ஆற்றாத யான் மறந்தால் இறந்துபடாது உளேன் ஆவது எத்தால்

en.1: What would become of me if I forgot? I don’t know how to forget, and even remembering burns my heart.
en.2: I don’t know how to forget that joy, and even as I remember it, parting burns my heart. I can’t bear parting as it is. If I forgot, how could I stay alive and not die?

uvacha.tr: Her friend says he will learn of her pain, come and give her joy. She answers.

padaccheda.m: தம்மை யான் எத்துணையும் மிகநினைந்தாலும் அதற்கு வெகுளார்
காதலர் எனக்குச் செய்யும் இன்பமாவது அவ்வளவன்றோ

en.1: However much I think of him, he doesn’t get angry. Isn’t that the honour my lover does me?
en.2: However much I think of him, he isn’t angry. He agrees to stay in my heart. Isn’t that all the joy my lover gives me? She knows no joy greater, so she calls it an honour. She is quietly mocking what her friend said.

uvacha.tr: She grieves that no messenger comes. Her friend urges her to be firm, and she answers.

padaccheda.w: வேறு அல்லம் என்பார் அளியின்மை ஆற்ற நினைந்து
padaccheda.m: முன்பெல்லாம் நாம் இருவரும் வேறல்லம் என்று சொல்லுவாரது அளியின்மையை மிகவும் நினைந்து
எனது இனியவுயிர் கழியாநின்றது

en.1: My sweet life is ending, as I dwell on the unkindness of the one who said, “We are not separate.”
en.2: My sweet life is going, as I think so much on the unkindness of the one who used to say, “We two are not separate.” His unkindness is leaving when he could come back, staying away and sending no messenger. It is his lack of loving-kindness, she answers her friend, not the parting, that is ending her life.

uvacha.tr: She has rejected her friend’s comfort. With desire at its height and her grief past bearing, she says this.

padaccheda.m: மதியே
என் நெஞ்சின் இடைவிடாதிருந்தே விட்டுப்போயினாரை, யான் என் கண்ணளவாயினும் எதிர்ப்படும்வகை நீ படாது ஒழிவாயாக

en.1: Long may you live, moon. Don’t set, so that my eyes may see the one who left without leaving me.
en.2: Moon, don’t set, so that I may meet with my eyes the one who stays always in my heart and yet has gone. Both of them look at the moon, so their eyes meet on it. She says “long may you live” because she is pleading. With another reading, the moon won’t set, so she can’t sleep and see him in a dream.

uvacha.tr: She has seen a message from him come to her in a dream, and she says this.

padaccheda.m: யான் வருந்துகின்றது அறிந்து, அது தீரக் காதலர் விடுத்த தூதினைக்கொண்டு என்மாட்டு வந்த கனவினுக்கு
யான் விருந்தாக யாதனைச் செய்வேன்

en.1: What feast can I give the dream that came with a message from my lover?
en.2: Knowing I suffer, my lover sent a message to end it, and the dream came to me carrying it. What can I do for it as my guest? A feast means the courtesies due to a guest, and she asks because she can see nothing that could be offered to a dream.

uvacha.tr: She has been thinking of sending him a message, and she says this.

padaccheda.m: துஞ்சாதுவருந்துகின்ற என் கயல்போலும் உண்கண்கள் யான் இரந்தால் துஞ்சுமாயின்
கனவிடைக் காதலரைக் காண்பேன், கண்டால் அவர்க்கு யான் ஆற்றியுளேனாய தன்மையை யானே விரியச் சொல்வேன்

en.1: If my eyes, carp-shaped and dark with kohl, would sleep when I beg them, I could tell the one who held me that I have survived.
en.2: My carp-like eyes won’t sleep. If they would sleep when I begged them, I would see my lover in a dream and tell him myself how I have endured the sickness of desire, in full, with all that a messenger would leave out or shorten. But the eyes won’t sleep, so it can’t be said. She calls them carp-like in grief for the beauty she has lost.

uvacha.tr: Her friend fears she can’t bear the separation. She answers that she can.

padaccheda.m: நனவின்கண் வந்து தலையளி செய்யாதாரை
யான் கனவின்கட் கண்ட காட்சியானே என் உயிருண்டாகாநின்றது

en.1: He shows me no kindness when I am awake, but I see him in dreams, and that is what keeps me alive.
en.2: He won’t come and show me kindness while I am awake, but seeing him in a dream keeps the life in me. With that sight I can bear this, so you needn’t worry.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நனவின்கண் வந்து தலையளி செய்யாதாரை அவர்சென்றுழி நாடிக்கொண்டுவந்து கனவு தருதலான்
அக்கனவின்கண்ணே எனக்கு இன்பம் உண்டாகாநின்றது

en.1: In dreams I have the joy of desire, because a dream seeks out the man who shows no kindness when I am awake and brings him to me.
en.2: A dream finds the place he went to and brings back the man who won’t come to me in waking life, and so I have joy in it. By nature he shows no kindness, yet the dream finds him, fetches him and makes him kind. With that dream I can bear this.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: முன் நனவின்கண் அவரைக்கண்டு நுகர்ந்த இன்பந்தானும் இனிதாயிற்று அப்பொழுதே
இன்று கனவின்கட் கண்டு நுகர்ந்த இன்பமும் அக்கண்டபொழுதே இனிதாயிற்று, அதனான் எனக்கு இரண்டும் ஒத்தன

en.1: Even seeing him awake was sweet only at that moment. The dream too is sweet only while I am seeing it.
en.2: The joy I had when I saw him awake was sweet at that time. The joy I have today from seeing him in a dream is sweet at that time too. So the two are equal to me. That was all I ever had before, and with this I can bear it now.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நனவு என்று சொல்லப்படுகின்ற ஒரு பாவி இல்லையாயின்
கனவின்கண் வந்துகூடிய காதலர் என்னைப் பிரியார்

en.1: If there were no such thing as waking, my lover would never leave me in my dreams.
en.2: If there were none of this wretch called waking, the lover who comes and joins me in a dream wouldn’t leave me. Waking breaks in, ends the dream and parts him from me, and the word “thing” shows how cruel it is. She is telling how she gets through by having him in dreams.

uvacha.tr: She wakes and he is gone. Remembering their union in the dream, she can’t bear it, and says this.

padaccheda.m: ஒருஞான்றும் நனவின்கண் வந்து தலையளி செய்யாத கொடியவர்
நாள்தோறும் கனவின்கண் வந்து நம்மை வருத்துவது எவ்வியைபுபற்றி

en.1: He is cruel, giving me no kindness when I am awake. Why does he torment me in my dreams?
en.2: This cruel man never once comes to show me kindness when I am awake. By what right does he come every day in dreams and torment me? He is cruel because he left and doesn’t think of coming back. In a dream he is on my shoulders, and when I wake he hides, and that hurts too. People say what isn’t there awake isn’t there in dreams, but we haven’t found it so.

uvacha.tr: Her friend has spoken ill of him to help her bear it. She defends him.

padaccheda.m: என்நெஞ்சு விடாது உறைகின்ற காதலர் யான் துஞ்சும்பொழுது வந்து என் தோள்மேலராய்
பின் விழிக்கும்பொழுது, விரைந்து பழைய நெஞ்சின்கண்ணராவர்

en.1: When I sleep, he is on my shoulders. When I wake, he rushes into my heart.
en.2: My lover never leaves my heart. When I sleep he comes and lies on my shoulders, and when I wake he hurries back into my heart, where he was before. She says he hurries because it is so harsh that he breaks off their union and vanishes. He has never once left me, so you have no cause to blame him.

uvacha.tr: She goes on defending him to her friend.

padaccheda.m: தமக்கொரு காதலர் இன்மையின் அவரைக் கனவிற்கண்டறியாத மகளிர்
தாமறிய நனவின்கண் வந்து நல்காத நங்காதலரை அன்பிலர் என நோவா நிற்பர்

en.1: Those who never see a lover in their dreams blame him for showing no kindness in waking life.
en.2: Women who have no lover of their own, and so have never seen one in a dream, blame my lover as lacking loving-kindness because he doesn’t come to me in waking life. She can’t bear the blame, and speaks as if of strangers. If they had lovers and saw them in dreams, they would know how he comforts me there, and wouldn’t blame him.

uvacha.tr: She goes on defending him to her friend.

padaccheda.m: இவ்வூரின்மகளிர் நனவின்கண் நம்மை நீத்தார் என்று நம்காதலரைக் கொடுமைகூறாநிற்பர்
அவர் கனவின்கண் நீங்காதுவருதல் கண்டறியாரோ

en.1: They say he left me in waking life. Do the people of this village not see him in their dreams?
en.2: The women of this village call my lover cruel, saying he has left me in waking life. Do they not know he comes to me in dreams and doesn’t leave? She says “of this village” to mark her friend as an outsider. If there were no difference between them, her friend would see what she sees and be content. Instead she calls him cruel.

uvacha.tr: She quarrels with the evening, and says this.

padaccheda.m: பொழுதே! நீ மாலையோ அல்லை= நீ முன்னாள்களின் வந்த மாலையோவெனின், அல்லை

இருந்தவாற்றான் அந்நாட்காதலரை மணந்த மகளிர் உயிரை உண்ணும் இறுதிக்காலமாய் இருந்தாய். முன்னாள்= கூடியிருந்தநாள். அந்நாள் மணந்தார் எனவே, பின் பிரிந்தாரதல் பெறுதும். வாழி என்பது குறிப்புச்சொல். "வாலிழை மகளிர் உயிர்ப்பொதி அவிழ்க்குங் காலை" (கலித்தொகை, நெய்தற்கலி-2)என்றாற்போல ஈண்டுப் பொதுமையாற் கூறப்பட்டது. வேலை என்பது ஆகுபெயர். வேலை என்பதற்கு வேலாய் இருந்தாய் என்பாரும் உளர்

en.1: Long may you live, hour. You are no evening, but the time that eats the lives of those who have wed.
en.2: Hour, you are not the evening of the days when we were together. You have become the final hour that eats the lives of women joined to their lovers then and parted now. “Long may you live” is irony. Some read the word for “time” as “spear”, so that she says: you are a spear.

uvacha.tr: She lays her own inner sorrow on the evening, and says this.

padaccheda.m: மயங்கிய மாலாய்
நீயும் எம்போலப் புன்கண் உடையாய் இருந்தாய்

padaccheda.w: நின் துணை எம் கேள் போல் வன்கண்ணதோ
padaccheda.m: நின் துணையும் எந்துணை போல வன்கண்மையுடையதோ, கூறுவாயாக

en.1: You are wretched, dim evening, long may you live. Is your mate as hard-hearted as mine?
en.2: Dim evening, where day and night run together, you too have lost your brightness, as I have. Tell me, is your mate as hard-hearted as mine? From that lost brightness she imagines it has a mate. “Long may you live” carries a hidden sense: you have hurt me, and you have found no joy yourself.

uvacha.tr: Her friend tells her she must bear it, and she answers.

padaccheda.m: காதலர் கூடிய நாளெல்லாம் என்முன் நடுக்கம் எய்திப் பசந்து வந்த மாலை
இந்நாள் எனக்கு இறந்துபாடு வந்துதோன்றி அதற்குளதாம் துன்பம் ஒருகாலைக்கொருகால் மிக வாரா நின்றது

en.1: Evening comes with cold budding and its light growing pale, and with it despair buds in me and pain grows.
en.2: On all the days I was with my lover, evening came before me trembling and pale. Today it brings death into view, and a loathing of life, and the pain of that grows from moment to moment. On the surface the words only say that evening comes cool and dim, but they suggest this. How am I to bear it?

reading.note: பனி can be cold or trembling, and he hears both: the surface sense is a cool, dim evening, and beneath it evening once trembled before her.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: காதலர் உள்ளபொழுதெல்லாம் என்னுயிர் தளிர்ப்ப வந்தமாலை
அவரி்ல்லாத இப்பொழுது
அஃது ஒழிந்துநிற்றலேயன்றிக் கொல்லுங் களரியிற் கொலைஞர் வருமாறு போல அவ்வுயிரைக் கோடற்கு வாராநின்றது

en.1: When my lover is away, evening comes like strangers to a killing ground.
en.2: While my lover was here, evening came and my life put out new shoots. Now he is gone, it doesn’t only stop doing that. It comes to take my life, as executioners with no compassion come to the killing ground. It used to be my friend and bring me joy, and today it is my enemy and brings me pain. How am I to bear it?

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: (காலையும், மாலையும் அவர் கூடியஞான்று போலாது இஞ்ஞான்று வேறுபட்டு வாராநின்றன அவற்றுள்) யான் காலைக்குச் செய்த உபகாரம் யாது
மாலைக்குச் செய்த அபகாரம் யாது

en.1: What good did I do the morning, and what harm did I do the evening?
en.2: Morning and evening both come differently now. What favour did I do the morning? When we were together it made me fear his leaving, and now it comes as a shore to the flood of night. What harm did I do the evening? It used to bring joy and now brings endless pain. Unlike morning, it hurts me through its own cruelty.

uvacha.tr: Her friend asks why she agreed to his leaving, if she is like this now. She answers.

padaccheda.m: முன்னெல்லாம் எனக்கு நட்பாய் இன்பம் செய்துபோந்த மாலை இன்று பகையாய்த் துன்பம்செய்தலை
காதலர் பிரிதற்குமுன்னே அறியப்பெற்றிலேன்

en.1: Before the one who wed me left, I never knew that evening brings pain.
en.2: Evening used to be my friend and bring me joy, and today it is my enemy and brings me pain. I didn’t know this before my lover left. If I had known it would change like this, I wouldn’t have agreed to his going.

uvacha.tr: Her friend asks why she suffers so at evening, and she answers.

padaccheda.m: இக்காமநோயாகிய பூ
காலைப்பொழுதின்கண் அரும்பி
பகற்பொழுதெல்லாம் பேர்அரும்பாய் முதிர்ந்து
மாலைப்பொழுதின்கண் மலராநிற்கும்

en.1: This sickness buds in the morning, fills out all day and flowers in the evening.
en.2: This sickness of desire is a flower. It buds in the morning, ripens all day into a full bud, and opens at evening. On waking she takes comfort in the union of her dream. As the day goes she forgets it and thinks of the parting. At evening she sees beasts and people drawn back to their mates, remembers her own joy, and can’t bear it.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: முன்னெல்லாம் இனியதாய்ப் போந்த ஆயன்குழல்
இதுபொழுது அழல்போலச் சுடுவதாய மாலைக்குத் தூதுமாய்
அது வந்து என்னைக் கொல்வுழிக் கொல்லும் படையும் ஆயிற்று

en.1: The cowherd’s flute is a messenger for the evening that burns like fire, and a weapon that kills.
en.2: The cowherd’s flute, once sweet, has become the messenger of evening, which now burns like fire, and the weapon that kills me when evening comes. It is a messenger because it announces evening in advance, and a weapon because it is the means of killing. If evening can burn by itself, what won’t it do with all this help?

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: (இதற்கு முன்னெல்லாம் யானே மயங்கி நோயுழந்தேன்) இனிக் கண்டாரும் மதி மருளும்வகை மாலை வரும்பொழுது
இப்பதி எல்லாம் மயங்கி நோயுழக்கும்

en.1: When evening spreads and reason reels, the town reels too, and suffers.
en.2: Until now I alone was bewildered and in pain. Now evening comes so that all who see it lose their reason, and this whole town will be bewildered and suffer. She thinks of evening as Death coming for her, and she means that she will die. Some read it as: when evening comes dim, my town’s reason is shaken and it suffers.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: காதலர் பிரிவைப் பொறுத்து இறந்துபடாதிருந்த என் உயிர்
இன்று பொருள் இயல்பே தமக்கு இயல்பாக உடையவரை நினைந்து, இம்மயங்கும் மாலைக்கண்ணே இறந்துபடாநின்றது

en.1: My life has not died yet, but in this dim evening it is dying, as I think of the man whose way is wealth.
en.2: My life, which bore his leaving and didn’t die, is dying in this dim evening as I think of him. The agreed season has passed and he stays away until his wealth is won. He has lost his own nature, of never changing his word, and taken on the nature of wealth. It has come to this, and nothing you say can help now.

uvacha.tr: She has changed, because the pain is more than she can bear. Her friend says this to her.

padaccheda.m: இவ்வாற்றாமை நம்கண்ணே நிற்பத் தாம் சேணிடைச் சென்ற காதலரை நீ நினைந்து அழுதலால்
நின்கண்கள் ஒளியிழந்து முன் தமக்கு நாணிய நறுமலர்கட்கு இன்று தாம் நாணிவிட்டன

en.1: He went far away and left us this misery. As you think of him, your eyes now shrink in shame before sweet flowers.
en.2: He went far away and left this misery with us. You think of him and weep, so your eyes have lost their light, and the fragrant flowers that were once ashamed before them now shame them. Anyone who sees this will call him cruel, so you must bear it.

uvacha.tr: Her friend goes on.

padaccheda.m: பசப்பெய்தன்மேல் நீர் வார்கின்ற நின்கண்கள்
நம்மான் நயக்கப்பட்டவரது நல்காமையைப் பிறர்க்குச் சொல்லுவபோலாநின்றன. இனி, நீ ஆற்றல் வேண்டும்

en.1: Your eyes, pale and streaming with tears, seem to be telling of the unkindness of the one you long for.
en.2: Your eyes have turned pale and now run with tears. They seem to tell others that the man we long for shows us no kindness, because from them people can infer it. So you must bear this. Some have a text in which the eyes tell him.

uvacha.tr: Her friend goes on.

padaccheda.m: காதலர் மணந்த ஞான்று இன்பம் மிகுதியாற் பூரித்த நின்தோள்கள்
இன்று அவர் பிரிந்தமையை விளங்க உணர்த்துவபோல மெலியாநின்றன, இது தகாது

en.1: Your arms, which swelled on the day he wed you, seem to be proclaiming that he has gone.
en.2: Your arms, which swelled with joy on the day he wed you, are thinning today as if to make his leaving plain. This is not right. If they swelled then and thin now, anyone who has seen both will soon understand, and will say he has no decency.

uvacha.tr: Her friend goes on.

padaccheda.m: அன்றும் துணைவர் நீங்குதலான் அவராற்பெற்ற செயற்கை அழகேயன்றிப் பழைய இயற்கை அழகும் இழந்த இ்ததோள்கள்
இன்று அதற்கும்மேலே தம் பெருமையிழந்து வளை கழலாநின்றன. இவை இங்ஙனம் செயற்பாலன அல்ல

en.1: With your companion gone, your arms have lost their old beauty. Now they shrink and the gold bangles slip away.
en.2: When your companion left, these arms lost the beauty he gave them and their old natural beauty too. Now they have lost their fullness as well, and the gold bangles slip off. They shouldn’t do this. Then they showed that he has no loving-kindness, and now that he lied, not coming in the agreed season. Can those who say so be blamed?

uvacha.tr: Her friend goes on.

padaccheda.m: கவவுக்கை நெகிழினும் ஆற்றாதாட்கு, இக்கால நீட்டத்து என்னாம் என்று நினையாத கொடியாரது கொடுமையைத் தாமே சொல்லாநின்றன
வளைகளும் கழன்று, பழைய இயற்கை அழகும் இழந்த இத்தோள்கள், இனி அதனை யாம் மறைக்குமாறு என்னை

en.1: Your arms, their bangles gone and their old beauty withered, tell of the cruelty of a cruel man.
en.2: You couldn’t bear it even when his embrace loosened, and the cruel man never thought what so long a time would do to you. These arms, their bangles gone and their old beauty lost, tell of his cruelty themselves, so how can we hide it? If the arms that held him say it, what need is there for outsiders to speak?

uvacha.tr: Her friend has blamed him to help her bear it. She answers.

padaccheda.m: யான் ஆற்றவும், என் வயத்தவன்றித் தொடிகள் கழலுமாறு தோள்கள் மெலிய
அவற்றைக்கண்டு நீ அவரைக் கொடியர் எனக் கூறுதலைப் பொறாது யான் என்னுள்ளே நோவாநின்றேன்

en.1: My arms grow thin and my bangles slip, and I ache to hear him called cruel.
en.2: I do bear it, but beyond my control my arms thin and my bangles slip. You see that and call him cruel, and I can’t stand it, and I ache inside. What I can’t bear isn’t his staying away. It is what you say.

uvacha.tr: She can’t bear to hear him blamed, and she says this to her heart.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே
இவள் கொடியார் என்கிறவர்க்கு, நீ சென்று என் மெலிகின்ற தோளினால் விளைகின்ற ஆரவாரத்தைச் சொல்லி
ஒரு மேம்பாடு எய்த வல்லையோ, வல்லையாயின் அதனை ஒப்பது இல்லை

en.1: Will you win glory, my heart, by telling that cruel man about the uproar over my wasting arms?
en.2: My heart, go to the man she calls cruel, tell him of the uproar over my wasting arms, and can you win some honour? If so, nothing could equal it. “Cruel” implies he isn’t, and the arms waste of themselves. Once he hears you he will come and all this will end, a good deed done in time, and you will have its whole reward.

uvacha.tr: His work is done and he is about to return. He remembers the past and says this to himself.

padaccheda.m: தன்னை இறுக முயங்கிய கைகளை, இவட்கு நோகும் என்று கருதி ஒருஞான்று யான் நெகிழ்த்தேனாக
அத்துணையும் பொறாது, பைந்தொடிகளை அணிந்த பேதையது நுதல் பசந்தது, அப்பெற்றித்தாய நுதல் இப்பிரிவிற்கு யாது செய்யுமோ

en.1: When I loosened my arms in our embrace, the forehead of that simple girl in gold bangles turned pale.
en.2: One day I loosened the arms that held her tight, thinking it would hurt her. She couldn’t bear even that, and the forehead of that simple girl in gold bangles turned pale. What will such a forehead do in this separation? I must go back quickly.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

padaccheda.m: அங்ஙனம் கைகளை ஊக்குதலான் அம்முயக்கிடையே சிறுகாற்று நுழைந்ததாக
அத்துணை இடையீடும் பொறாது, பேதையுடைய பெரிய மழைக்கண்கள் பசப்புற்றன

en.1: When a cool breeze cut through our embrace, the simple girl’s great rain-cool eyes turned pale.
en.2: As I loosened my arms, a small breeze slipped in between us. Her large cool eyes couldn’t bear even that gap and turned pale. How have such eyes borne all that lies between us now, the mountains, forests and lands? “Cut through” shows that the two bodies had become one.

uvacha.tr: He goes on, to himself.

padaccheda.m: தண்வளி போழவந்த கண்ணின் பசப்புத் துன்பம் உற்றது
தனக்கு அயலாய ஒண்ணுநல் விளைத்த பசப்பைக்கண்டு

en.1: Even the pallor in her eyes suffered when it saw what her bright forehead had done.
en.2: The pallor in her eyes suffered when it saw the pallor made by her bright forehead. The forehead paled as soon as my arms loosened. The eyes paled only when a breeze came between us, and they were ashamed of their hardness beside its tenderness. So her features race each other to lose their beauty, and I must hurry.

uvacha.tr: She asks how her suffering might be ended.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே
இவ் எவ்வநோயினைத் தீர்க்கும் மருந்தாவது ஒன்றனை
யான் அறியும் ஆ்றறல் இலன், எத்தன்மையது யாதொன்றாயினும் நீ அறிந்து எனக்குச் சொல்

en.1: Won’t you think of something, heart, and tell me any cure at all for this unending sickness?
en.2: My heart, I haven’t the power to find it. Whatever it may be, find out and tell me one medicine for this sickness that nothing relieves. “Any at all” means even something that gives up modesty, which is worth more than life.

uvacha.tr: Her longing to see him overwhelms her, and she says this.

padaccheda.m: என் நெஞ்சே வாழ்வாயாக
அவர் நம்கண் காதல் இலராகவும் நீ அவர் வரவு நோக்கி வருந்துதற்கு ஏது
நின் பேதைமையே பிறிதில்லை

en.1: He has no love for you, yet you go on suffering. That is foolishness, my heart, long may you live.
en.2: He has no love for us, yet you suffer, waiting for him to come. That is your own foolishness and nothing else. He doesn’t think of us, so we can tell he has no love, and you don’t see that. You don’t think of going to him either, and you bring this on yourself. “Long may you live” is mockery. The wise thing is for us to go to him.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே! அவர்பாற் செல்வதும் செய்யாது, ஈண்டு இறந்துபடுவதும் செய்யாது இருந்து அவர் வரவுநினைந்து நீ வருந்துகின்றது என்னை

padaccheda.w: பைதல் நோய் செய்தார்கண் பரிந்து உள்ளல் இல்
padaccheda.m: இப்பையுள் நோய் செய்தார்மாட்டு நமக்கு இரங்கி வரக்கருதுதல் உண்டாகாது

en.1: Why sit here thinking of him and aching, heart? The one who gave us this sickness of grief has no tender thought for us.
en.2: My heart, you neither go to him nor die here. Why sit thinking of his return and suffering? The man who gave us this sickness of grief won’t think of us with pity and come. He has no compassion for us, so he won’t come of himself. It is right now that we go to him.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே, நீ அவர்பால் சேறலுற்றாயாயின் இக்கண்களையும் உடன் கொண்டு செல்வாயாக
அன்றி நீ சேறியாயின், இவைதாம் காட்சிவிதுப்பினால் அவரைக் காண்டல்வேண்டி நீ காட்டு என்று என்னைத் தின்பனபோன்று நலியாநிற்கும்

en.1: Take my eyes with you too when you go, heart. Wanting to see him, they are eating me.
en.2: My heart, if you go to him, take these eyes with you. If you go without them, their craving will torment me as if devouring me, demanding that I show him to them. She wants that torment ended, which means she herself intends to go.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: நெஞ்சே! யாம் உற்றால் உறாஅதவர்= யாம் நம்மையுறத் தாமுறாத நம் காதலரை
வெறுத்தார் என்று கருதிப் புலந்து கைவிட்டிருக்கும் வலி நமக்கு உண்டோ, இல்லை

en.1: We are drawn to him and he isn’t drawn to us. Can we give him up as an enemy, heart?
en.2: He doesn’t return the loving-kindness we give him. Do we have the strength to decide he hates us, sulk and give him up? We don’t. Since we lack that strength, the right thing for us is to go to him.

uvacha.tr: Her heart thinks of his cruelty and won’t agree to go. She scolds it.

padaccheda.m: என்னெஞ்சே!: கலந்து உணர்த்தும் காதலர்க் கண்டாற்புலந்து உணராய்= யான் தம்மொடு புலந்தால், அப்புலவியைக் கலவிதன்னானே நீக்கவல்ல காதலரைக் காண்டாற் பொய்யேயாயினும் ஒருகாற் புலந்து பின்அதனை நீங்க மாட்டாய்
அதுவும் மாட்டாத நீ, இப்பொழுது அவர் கொடியர் எனப் பொய்க்காய்வு காயாநின்றாய், இனி அதனை ஒழிந்து அவர்பால் செல்லத் துணிவாயாக

en.1: When you see the lover who mends a sulk with an embrace, you can’t even sulk. Your anger now is a pretence, my heart.
en.2: If I sulk, my lover can end it by making love. When you see him, you can’t sulk even once in pretence and then give it up. You can’t do that, yet now you rage at him as cruel. That is false anger with no firmness in it. If you fail when you see him, hating him when you don’t is useless. Stop, and make up your mind to go to him.

uvacha.tr: Her modesty holds her back, so she gives up going, and she says this.

padaccheda.m: நல்ல நெஞ்சே
ஒன்றின் நாண்விட மாட்டாயாயின் காம வேட்கையை விடு
ஒன்றின் அது விடமாட்டாயாயின், நாணினை விடு
அன்றியே இரண்டும் விடாமை நின்கருத்தாயின், ஒன்றற்கொன்று மறுதலையாய இவ்விரண்டனையும் உடன்தாங்கு மதுகை யான்இலன்

en.1: Good heart, give up desire or give up modesty. I can’t bear them both.
en.2: Good heart, if you won’t give up modesty, give up desire. If you won’t give up that, give up modesty. If you mean to keep both, I haven’t the strength to carry two opposites at once, even if you have. She calls the heart good because keeping both preserves a woman’s womanhood. That is good, but her life can’t stand it.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: என் நெஞ்சே
அவர் இவ்வாற்றையை அறியாமையின் நொந்துவந்து தலையளி செய்யார் ஆயினார் என்று கருதி
அஃது அறிவித்தற் பொரு்ட்டு, நம்மைப் பிரிந்துபோயவர்பின் ஏங்கிச் செல்லலுற்ற நீ யாதும் அறியாய்

en.1: You pine because he won’t show tender kindness, and you go after the one who left. You are a fool, my heart.
en.2: My heart, you think he shows no kindness only because he doesn’t know how I suffer, and you would go pining after him to tell him. You know nothing. He saw my suffering and left without kindness. It is foolish to think he will come just because you told him, away from the sight of it.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her heart.

padaccheda.m: என்னெஞ்சே
காதலர் நின் அகத்தாராக
முன்பு எல்லாம் கண்டுவைத்து இப்பொழுது நீ புறத்துத் தேடிச் செல்கின்றது யாரிடத்து

en.1: Your lover is within you, my heart. Whom are you thinking of, and to whom are you going?
en.2: My heart, your lover is inside you. You have seen it all before, so who is it you go searching for outside? To go looking outside for someone who lives within you, not knowing it, is laughable. Give it up.

uvacha.tr: She says this to mean that she must forget him and bear it.

padaccheda.m: நம்மைக் கூடாவண்ணம் துறந்துபோயினாரை நாம் நம் அகத்து உடையேமாக
முன் இழந்த புறக்கவினேயன்றி நின்ற அகக்கவினும் இழப்பேம்

en.1: If we keep in our heart the one who left us and won’t come near, we will lose still more of our beauty.
en.2: He left us so that we can’t be together. If we keep him within us, we will lose the inner beauty that remains as well as the outer beauty already gone. He has left and won’t come near us, and we can’t forget him, so we will lose even the composure we still have.

uvacha.tr: Her friend tells her to bear it, so that her modesty and reserve aren’t lost. She answers.

padaccheda.m: நாணாகிய தாழினைக் கோத்த நிறையென்னும் கதவினை
காமவேட்கையாகிய கணிச்சி முறியாநின்றது, இனி அவை நிற்றலும் இல்லை, யான் ஆற்றலும் இல்லை,

en.1: The axe of desire breaks down the door of reserve, bolted with modesty.
en.2: The axe of desire is breaking the door of reserve, on which modesty is the bolt. Neither can stand now, and I can’t bear this. While modesty lasts reserve won’t fail, so it is the bolt. Reserve keeps what is inside from others, so it is the door. Both are strong and won’t go of themselves, but her longing removes them together, so it is the axe.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says desire born in the heart can be held down by the heart. She answers.

padaccheda.m: எல்லாரும் தொழில் ஒழியும் இடையாமத்தும் என் நெஞ்சத்தை ஒறுத்துத் தொழில்கொள்ளாநின்றது
ஆகலான் காமம் என்று சொல்லப்பட்ட ஒன்று கண்ணோட்டம் இன்றாய் இருந்தது

en.1: This thing called desire has no mercy. Even in the dead of night it rules my heart and puts it to work.
en.2: Even at midnight, when everyone stops work, it punishes my heart and works it, so the thing called desire has no kindly regard. The work is sending her heart to him. Desire was born in her heart, and putting your mother to work isn’t the way of the world, so she says “a thing called desire”. She means it can’t be held down.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says women can hide desire. She answers.

padaccheda.m: இக்காமத்தை யான் என்னுள்ளே மறைக்கக் கருதுவேன்
அதனால் என், இஃது என்கருத்தின் வாராது தும்மல்போல வெளிப்பட்டே விடாநின்றது,

en.1: I would hide my desire, but it comes out without warning, like a sneeze.
en.2: I mean to hide this desire inside me, but what use is that? It breaks out against my will, like a sneeze. It can’t be held in, any more than a sneeze can.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: இன்றின் ஊங்கெ்ல்லாம் யான் என்னை நிறையுடையேன் என்று கருதியிருந்தேன்
அதனால் என், இன்று என்காமம் மறைத்தலைக் கடந்து மன்றின்கண் வெளிப்படாநின்றது

en.1: I used to say I had reserve. Now my desire has gone past hiding, out into the public square.
en.2: Until today I thought I had reserve. What use was that? Today my desire has gone past hiding and come out in the public square, so that many people know it. It is no longer in my power.

uvacha.tr: Her friend says they should forget the man who has forgotten them. She answers.

padaccheda.m: தம்மை அகன்றுசென்றார் பின் செல்லாது தாமும் அகன்றுநிற்கும் நிறையுடைமை
காமநோயினை உறாதார் அறிவது ஒன்றன்றி உற்றார் அறிவது ஒன்றன்று

en.1: The great dignity of not going after those who hurt you is not something known to people with the sickness of desire.
en.2: The reserve that doesn’t follow those who left, but keeps away from them in turn, is known only to people of pride who don’t have the sickness of desire. She says “hurt” because he makes time that should pass in joy pass in pain. Going after him means thinking of him without a break. My heart goes even to one who doesn’t value it, and I know no other way.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: என்னை அகன்று சென்றார் பின்னே யான் சேறலை வேண்டுதலான்
என்னை உற்றதுயர் எத்தன்மையது, சால நன்று

en.1: It makes me want to go after the one who hurt me. What a fine thing, this sorrow that has come to me!
en.2: What kind of sorrow has come to me, making me want to go after the one who left me? A very fine one! “Fine” is scorn. She means this sickness of desire can’t be spoken of or listened to, and is utterly cruel.

uvacha.tr: He came back from a courtesan, and she lost her reserve and went to him. Her friend asks why she didn’t sulk, and she answers.

padaccheda.m: நம்மால் விரும்பப்பட்டவர் வந்து, காமத்தால் நாம் விரும்பியவற்றைச் செய்யுமளவின்
நாண் என்று ஒன்றையும் அறியமாட்டேமாய் இருந்தேம்

en.1: When the one we cherish does, in desire, all we long for, we don’t even know there is such a thing as modesty.
en.2: When the man I desired came and, in desire, did what I longed for, we knew nothing at all of modesty. Modesty here is shame at touching a chest that courtesans have touched. What she longed for is the lovemaking her craving had dwelt on. Seeing her own fault in joining him unthinkingly, she says “we”, to include her friend.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நம் நிறையாகி அவர் அணை அழிக்கும் தானை
பல பொய்களை வல்ல கள்வனுடைய தாழ்ந்த சொற்கள் அன்றோ

en.1: Aren’t the humble words of that thief of many tricks the army that breaks down our womanhood?
en.2: The army that destroys the wall of our reserve is the humble talk of this thief, skilled in many lies, so how could it stand? Womanhood here means reserve. I had planned to sulk and not give way, but he came so that it all vanished and I was ahead of him in union. His humble words claim he has more loving-kindness than I do.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: அவர் வந்தபொழுது புலக்கக்கடவேன் என்று கருதி முன் நில்லாது பிறிது ஓர் இடத்துப் போயினேன்
போயும், என்னெஞ்சம் நிறையில்லாது அறைபோய் அவரோடு கலத்தல் தொடங்குதலை அறிந்து, இனி அது வாயாது என்று புல்லினேன்

en.1: I went off meaning to sulk. I saw my heart was ready to join him, and I embraced him.
en.2: Meaning to sulk when he came, I went off somewhere else and didn’t stand before him. But my heart, with no reserve, betrayed me and began to join him. Seeing that, I knew sulking wouldn’t work, and I embraced him. The heart is the means of sulking, and it had become the means of union.

uvacha.tr: She goes on, to her friend.

padaccheda.m: நிணத்தைத் தீயின்கண்ணே இட்டால், அஃது உருகுமாறுபோலத் தம் காதலரைக் கண்டால் நிறையழிந்து உருகும் நெஞ்சினையுடைய மகளிர்க்கு
அவர் புணர யாம் ஊடிப் பின்பு உணராது அந்நிலையே நிற்கக்கடவேம் என்று கருதுதல் உண்டாகுமோ, ஆகாது

en.1: Can those whose hearts are like fat in a fire say, when they come together, that they will hold to their sulk?
en.2: Fat put in a fire melts, and so do the hearts of women when they see their lovers, and their reserve is gone. When he draws close, can such women think they will sulk and stay that way without relenting? They can’t. Coming together here means coming very near, or meeting. I am such a woman, so sulking wasn’t possible for me.

uvacha.tr: She is eager to see him, and she says this.
